problems.title: Top 3 earners in each department
problems.question: Table employees(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary). Return the top 3 earners in each department. What happens when two people tie on salary?
problems.answer:
SELECT emp_id, name, dept_id, salary
FROM employees
QUALIFY DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) <= 3;

Portable version (no QUALIFY):

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.*,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees e
)
SELECT emp_id, name, dept_id, salary FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 3;

The tie decision is the real question. Salaries 100, 100, 90, 80:

function values rows returned for "≤ 3"
ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3,4 exactly 3 rows — one tied person is dropped arbitrarily
RANK 1,1,3,4 3 rows (100,100,90) — skips 2
DENSE_RANK 1,1,2,3 4 rows — top 3 distinct salaries

Say which you chose and why. "Top 3 people" → RANK; "top 3 salary levels" → DENSE_RANK; "exactly 3 rows" → ROW_NUMBER with a tie-breaker (ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id) so results are deterministic.
problems.lookfor:
• Asking about ties before writing code
  • Knowing QUALIFY (Snowflake, also BigQuery/Databricks/DuckDB)
  • Adding a tie-breaker to ROW_NUMBER — non-deterministic results are a classic production bug
problems.followup: How would you return departments with fewer than 3 employees too, plus the department name, including departments with zero employees? (LEFT JOIN departments, rank in a CTE, filter rnk <= 3 OR rnk IS NULL.)

problems.title: Employees who joined in the last 6 months
problems.question: employees(emp_id, name, hire_date DATE). List employees who joined in the last 6 months.
problems.answer:
SELECT emp_id, name, hire_date
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= DATEADD(month, -6, CURRENT_DATE)
  AND hire_date <= CURRENT_DATE;   -- excludes future-dated joiners

Points to say out loud:

  • Keep the column bare (hire_date >= <expression>). Writing DATEDIFF(month, hire_date, CURRENT_DATE) <= 6 wraps the column in a function, which hurts partition pruning on large tables — and DATEDIFF(month, …) counts month boundaries crossed, not elapsed months (Jan 31 → Feb 1 = 1 month).
  • "6 months" is ambiguous: rolling 6 months from today, or the last 6 complete calendar months? Calendar version: hire_date >= DATEADD(month, -6, DATE_TRUNC(month, CURRENT_DATE)) AND hire_date < DATE_TRUNC(month, CURRENT_DATE)
  • If the column is a TIMESTAMP_TZ/LTZ, CURRENT_DATE depends on the session TIMEZONE parameter.
problems.lookfor: Clarifying the definition, sargable predicates, awareness of DATEDIFF boundary semantics and time zones.
problems.followup: Count joiners per month for the last 12 months, showing 0 for months with no joiners (needs a date spine — see the date-spine problem).

problems.title: Running salary total per employee
problems.question: salary_history(emp_id, pay_date, amount). For each employee, show each payment and the running total of what they've been paid so far.
problems.answer:
SELECT emp_id, pay_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY emp_id
         ORDER BY pay_date
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_total
FROM salary_history
ORDER BY emp_id, pay_date;

The trap: the default frame. With ORDER BY and no frame clause, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE treats rows with the same pay_date as peers, so two payments on the same date both show the total including each other — the running total jumps and repeats. Writing ROWS explicitly (and adding a tie-breaker such as ORDER BY pay_date, payment_id) gives a true row-by-row total.

Same pattern, other questions they ask:

  • 3-payment moving average: AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY emp_id ORDER BY pay_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
  • Year-to-date: add DATE_TRUNC(year, pay_date) to the PARTITION BY.
problems.lookfor: Knowing ROWS vs RANGE and the default frame — this separates people who use window functions from people who understand them.
problems.followup: Why might LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY emp_id ORDER BY pay_date) return the current row's value instead of the last one? (Same default frame — needs ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.)

problems.title: Departments with more than 5 employees
problems.question: employees(emp_id, dept_id), departments(dept_id, dept_name). Which departments have more than 5 employees? Show the name.
problems.answer:
SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS headcount
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) > 5;

Discussion points:

  • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. You can't use COUNT() in WHERE.
  • If the table can contain the same employee twice (history table), use COUNT(DISTINCT e.emp_id).
  • If they then ask for "all departments with their headcount, including empty ones": LEFT JOIN and COUNT(e.emp_id) (not COUNT(*), which would count the NULL row as 1).
  • Subquery version they may ask for: WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).
problems.lookfor: WHERE vs HAVING, COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) with outer joins, handling duplicates.
problems.followup: Return the department(s) with the highest headcount, including ties. (QUALIFY RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) = 1 after GROUP BY — window functions run after aggregation.)

problems.title: Deduplicate rows without DISTINCT
problems.question: A raw table customers_raw(customer_id, email, updated_at, …) has duplicates. (a) Select one row per customer — the latest. (b) Actually remove the duplicates from the table in Snowflake, without DISTINCT.
problems.answer:
(a) Select latest per key:

SELECT *
FROM customers_raw
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY customer_id
          ORDER BY updated_at DESC, _loaded_at DESC   -- tie-breaker!
        ) = 1;

(b) Remove duplicates in place. Snowflake has no ROWID, so the classic Oracle DELETE … WHERE rowid NOT IN (…) doesn't work. Options:

-- Option 1: rewrite the table atomically (keeps grants, table identity)
INSERT OVERWRITE INTO customers_raw
SELECT * FROM customers_raw
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                           ORDER BY updated_at DESC, _loaded_at DESC) = 1;

-- Option 2: build a clean copy and swap
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE customers_clean AS
SELECT * FROM customers_raw
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1;
ALTER TABLE customers_raw SWAP WITH customers_clean;

For exact duplicates (every column identical) ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY <all columns> ORDER BY NULL) works, or SELECT … GROUP BY <all columns>.

Senior-level additions:

  • Fix the cause, not just the symptom: why are duplicates arriving (at-least-once delivery, re-loaded files, retries)? Make the load idempotent (MERGE on key, or delete+insert per batch).
  • Large tables: Option 1 rewrites every micro-partition — schedule it, or dedupe only recent partitions with a date filter.
  • CREATE OR REPLACE drops Time Travel history of the original object and grants (unless COPY GRANTS); INSERT OVERWRITE keeps the object.
problems.lookfor: Deterministic tie-breaker, knowing Snowflake lacks ROWID, atomic rewrite, and talking about root cause/idempotency.
problems.followup: How do you find which columns differ between duplicate rows for the same key? (COUNT(DISTINCT col) per key for each column, or HASH(*)/HASH_AGG.)

problems.title: Employees earning above their department's average
problems.question: Return employees whose salary is above the average salary of their own department.
problems.answer:
-- Window version: one pass over the table
SELECT emp_id, name, dept_id, salary
FROM employees
QUALIFY salary > AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id);

-- Join version (what "using joins & subqueries" expects)
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary, d.avg_sal
FROM employees e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
      FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id) d
  ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal;

Notes:

  • The correlated subquery (WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id)) is also correct; modern optimisers usually decorrelate it, but the window/join versions state intent clearly.
  • AVG ignores NULL salaries — say whether NULLs should count as 0.
  • If employees can have dept_id IS NULL, the window version groups them together as one "department"; the join version drops them.
problems.lookfor: Two approaches, and awareness of NULL behaviour.
problems.followup: Show each employee's difference from the department median, not the average. (MEDIAN(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) in Snowflake.)

problems.title: Turn 1,1,1,0,0,0 into 1,0,1,0,1,0
problems.question: A table has one column col with values 1,1,1,0,0,0. Write a query that outputs them alternating: 1,0,1,0,1,0.
problems.answer:
A common answer is:

SELECT CASE WHEN ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY col) % 2 = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
FROM t;

That's a trap answer — it never reads the data. It prints 1,0,1,0… regardless of what's in the table (try it on six 1s). Interviewers ask this to see if you reorder the actual rows.

Correct approach: number each value within its own group, then interleave.

SELECT col AS alternating_values
FROM (
  SELECT col,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY col ORDER BY col) AS rn
  FROM t
)
ORDER BY rn, col DESC;

How it works: the 1s get rn = 1,2,3 and the 0s get rn = 1,2,3. Sorting by rn puts pairs together (1st 1, 1st 0, 2nd 1, 2nd 0…), and col DESC puts the 1 before the 0 in each pair.

If counts are unequal (four 1s, two 0s), this gives 1,0,1,0,1,1 — the extras land at the end, which is the sensible behaviour. Mention it.
problems.lookfor: Recognising that the output must come from the data, PARTITION BY inside ROW_NUMBER, and that SQL tables are unordered — only ORDER BY in the final query guarantees order.
problems.followup: Interleave three categories A, B, C in round-robin order. (Same idea: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category …), then ORDER BY rn, category.)

problems.title: Nth highest salary, with ties and missing values
problems.question: Return the 2nd highest distinct salary in the company. If there isn't one, return NULL (not an empty result).
problems.answer:
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest      -- MAX over 0 rows returns NULL, not 0 rows
FROM (
  SELECT salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
)
WHERE rnk = 2;

Why each part:

  • DENSE_RANK so that 100,100,90 gives 90 as 2nd (with ROW_NUMBER you'd get 100).
  • Wrapping in MAX() turns "no row" into one NULL row — the requirement.
  • Classic alternatives: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees) (only works for N=2), or SELECT DISTINCT salary … ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 (returns 0 rows if missing).
problems.lookfor: Distinct vs positional ranking, the empty-result requirement, generalising to N.
problems.followup: Nth highest per department, as a reusable query where N is a parameter (SET n = 3; then rnk = $n).

problems.title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
problems.question:
SELECT customer_id FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);

This returns zero rows, although many customers have never ordered. Why? Fix it.
problems.answer:
orders.customer_id contains at least one NULL. x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) expands to x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL. x <> NULL is UNKNOWN, so the whole condition is never TRUE → no rows.

Fixes:

-- NOT EXISTS: NULL-safe and usually the best anti-join
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);

-- LEFT JOIN anti-join
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;

-- or filter NULLs inside NOT IN
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL)

Related NULL facts worth saying: NULL = NULL is not TRUE (use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM or EQUAL_NULL in Snowflake for NULL-safe equality); IN (…, NULL) is fine for positive matches.
problems.lookfor: Three-valued logic explained clearly, and a default habit of NOT EXISTS.
problems.followup: What does COUNT(*) WHERE col <> 'X' miss? (Rows where col is NULL.)

problems.title: LEFT JOIN that silently became an INNER JOIN
problems.question:
"List all customers and their 2026 orders (customers with no 2026 orders should still appear)."

SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-01-01';

Customers without 2026 orders are missing. Why?
problems.answer:
For customers with no matching order, o.order_date is NULL. The WHERE clause runs after the join and NULL >= '2026-01-01' is not TRUE, so those rows are removed — it behaves like an inner join.

Put conditions on the right-hand table in the ON clause:

SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
 AND o.order_date >= '2026-01-01';

Rule of thumb: filters on the preserved (left) table go in WHERE; filters on the optional (right) table go in ON. The exception is the deliberate anti-join, WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL.
problems.lookfor: Order of evaluation (FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window → QUALIFY → SELECT → ORDER BY) and the ON-vs-WHERE rule.
problems.followup: Same customers, but show the count of 2026 orders, 0 for none. (COUNT(o.order_id) with the filter in ON.)

problems.title: COUNT(*), COUNT(col), COUNT(DISTINCT) and AVG with NULLs
problems.question: Column bonus has values: 100, NULL, 100, 200, NULL (5 rows). What do COUNT(*), COUNT(bonus), COUNT(DISTINCT bonus), SUM(bonus), AVG(bonus) return? What's the "average bonus per employee"?
problems.answer:
expression result why
COUNT(*) 5 counts rows
COUNT(bonus) 3 ignores NULLs
COUNT(DISTINCT bonus) 2 100, 200
SUM(bonus) 400 ignores NULLs
AVG(bonus) 133.33 400 / 3 — NULLs excluded from the denominator

"Average bonus per employee" probably means 400 / 5 = 80, i.e. AVG(COALESCE(bonus, 0)) or SUM(bonus) / COUNT(*). Ask whether NULL means "no bonus" (= 0) or "unknown" (exclude). That's a business question, not a SQL one.

Also: SUM over zero rows (or all NULLs) returns NULL, not 0 — wrap in COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) for reports. COUNT never returns NULL.
problems.lookfor: Precise NULL behaviour and turning it into a business clarification.
problems.followup: COUNT(DISTINCT a, b) in Snowflake — does it count rows where a or b is NULL? (No: rows with any NULL in the listed columns are excluded.)

problems.title: Longest streak of consecutive login days (gaps and islands)
problems.question: logins(user_id, login_ts TIMESTAMP) — users may log in several times a day. For each user, find their longest streak of consecutive days with at least one login, with its start and end dates.
problems.answer:
WITH days AS (                      -- 1. one row per user per day
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_ts::DATE AS d
  FROM logins
),
grp AS (                            -- 2. island key: date minus its row number
  SELECT user_id, d,
         DATEADD(day,
                 -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d),
                 d) AS island
  FROM days
),
streaks AS (                        -- 3. one row per island
  SELECT user_id, island,
         MIN(d) AS start_date, MAX(d) AS end_date, COUNT(*) AS days
  FROM grp
  GROUP BY user_id, island
)
SELECT user_id, start_date, end_date, days
FROM streaks
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                           ORDER BY days DESC, start_date DESC) = 1;

Why step 2 works: for consecutive dates, the date and its row number both go up by 1, so date − row_number stays constant. A gap breaks the constant, starting a new island.

d rn d − rn
Mar 1 1 Feb 28
Mar 2 2 Feb 28
Mar 3 3 Feb 28
Mar 6 4 Mar 2 ← new island

Alternative: LAG(d) to flag d − prev_d > 1 as a new-island start, then a running SUM of flags as the island id. Same result, works when the "gap" rule is more complex (e.g. "gap > 2 days").

The DISTINCT in step 1 is essential — duplicate days would break the arithmetic.
problems.lookfor: Naming the pattern ("gaps and islands"), explaining why the subtraction works, deduping first.
problems.followup: Current streak only (islands ending today or yesterday)? Streaks allowing one missed day? (Use the LAG + running-sum version with gap > 2.)

problems.title: Sessionize clickstream with a 30-minute inactivity rule
problems.question: events(user_id, event_ts, page). A new session starts when a user has been inactive for more than 30 minutes. Assign a session_id to every event and report session start, end, duration and event count.
problems.answer:
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT e.*,
         CASE
           WHEN LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) IS NULL
             OR DATEDIFF(second,
                         LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts),
                         event_ts) > 30*60
           THEN 1 ELSE 0
         END AS is_new_session
  FROM events e
),
numbered AS (
  SELECT f.*,
         SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts
                                   ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_seq
  FROM flagged f
)
SELECT user_id,
       user_id || '-' || session_seq                AS session_id,
       MIN(event_ts)                                 AS session_start,
       MAX(event_ts)                                 AS session_end,
       DATEDIFF(second, MIN(event_ts), MAX(event_ts)) AS duration_sec,
       COUNT(*)                                      AS events
FROM numbered
GROUP BY user_id, session_seq;

The pattern — flag the start of each group with LAG, then a running SUM of flags gives a group number — solves many problems: sessions, "status changed" runs, consecutive failures, etc.

Production notes for a data architect answer:

  • In an incremental pipeline, sessions can span batch boundaries. Reprocess a lookback window (e.g. events from the last open session per user), or keep "open session" state.
  • Use ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING explicitly, and add a tie-breaker (event_id) if timestamps can collide.
problems.lookfor: The flag + running-sum pattern, and spotting the incremental/batch-boundary issue.
problems.followup: Average session length per user per day, and the % of sessions with only one event (bounce rate).

problems.title: Month-over-month revenue growth
problems.question: orders(order_id, order_ts, amount). Show monthly revenue and month-over-month growth %.
problems.answer:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC(month, order_ts)::DATE AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 2) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

Traps to call out:

  • Missing months. If March had no orders, LAG compares April to February. Join to a month spine first (see the date-spine problem) and COALESCE(revenue, 0).
  • Division by zero: NULLIF(prev, 0) (or Snowflake's DIV0/DIV0NULL).
  • Integer division in some databases (7/2 = 3) — not in Snowflake, but mention casting.
  • Year-over-year: LAG(revenue, 12) only works if the spine guarantees one row per month.
problems.lookfor: Handling gaps, safe division, and knowing LAG(x, n).
problems.followup: Rolling 3-month revenue and its growth vs the previous 3 months.

problems.title: Fill in missing dates with a date spine
problems.question: Daily sales exist only for days with sales. Produce one row for every day of 2026 with 0 for days without sales.
problems.answer:
-- Snowflake: GENERATOR (fast, no recursion)
WITH spine AS (
  SELECT DATEADD(day, SEQ4(), '2026-01-01'::DATE) AS d
  FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 366))
  QUALIFY d < '2027-01-01'
)
SELECT s.d, COALESCE(SUM(x.amount), 0) AS sales
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN sales x ON x.sale_date = s.d
GROUP BY s.d
ORDER BY s.d;

Gotcha: SEQ4() can have gaps in edge cases. For a guaranteed gap-free sequence use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1.

Portable recursive version:

WITH RECURSIVE spine(d) AS (
  SELECT '2026-01-01'::DATE
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DATEADD(day, 1, d) FROM spine WHERE d < '2026-12-31'
)
SELECT … FROM spine LEFT JOIN …

In a dbt project, the answer is usually "we have a dim_date model" (or dbt_utils.date_spine). Mention that a reusable calendar dimension also carries fiscal periods, holidays, week numbers.
problems.lookfor: Knowing a spine is needed, LEFT JOIN from the spine, and the dimension-table answer.
problems.followup: Every (store, day) combination with 0 for missing — CROSS JOIN stores to the spine first.

problems.title: Median and percentiles
problems.question: Find the median order value per country, and the 90th percentile. What's the difference between PERCENTILE_CONT and PERCENTILE_DISC? What would you use on 10 billion rows?
problems.answer:
SELECT country,
       MEDIAN(amount)                                          AS median_amt,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount)     AS p90_interpolated,
       PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY amount)     AS p90_actual_value
FROM orders
GROUP BY country;
  • PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates between values (median of 10, 20 = 15).
  • PERCENTILE_DISC returns an actual value from the data (10 or 20).
  • MEDIAN(x) = PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5).
  • At very large scale: APPROX_PERCENTILE(amount, 0.9) (t-digest) — small memory, mergeable, tiny error. Same idea as APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (HyperLogLog) vs COUNT(DISTINCT).

Without a median function (classic interview): rank rows ascending and descending; the median rows are where ABS(asc_rn - desc_rn) <= 1, then average them.
problems.lookfor: CONT vs DISC, approximate functions for scale, and the manual technique if asked.
problems.followup: Median per country as a window function next to each order (MEDIAN(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY country)).

problems.title: Customers who bought product A but never product B
problems.question: purchases(customer_id, product). Find customers who bought 'A' but never 'B'.
problems.answer:
-- 1. Conditional aggregation: one scan, easy to extend
SELECT customer_id
FROM purchases
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT_IF(product = 'A') > 0
   AND COUNT_IF(product = 'B') = 0;

-- 2. EXISTS / NOT EXISTS
SELECT DISTINCT p.customer_id
FROM purchases p
WHERE p.product = 'A'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM purchases q
                  WHERE q.customer_id = p.customer_id AND q.product = 'B');

-- 3. Set operation
SELECT customer_id FROM purchases WHERE product = 'A'
EXCEPT            -- MINUS in Snowflake/Oracle
SELECT customer_id FROM purchases WHERE product = 'B';

COUNT_IF is Snowflake; portable is SUM(CASE WHEN product='A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). Version 1 is the most flexible ("bought A and C but not B" = one more line).
problems.lookfor: Multiple approaches, and knowing EXCEPT removes duplicates.
problems.followup: Customers who bought every product in a products table (relational division: HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products)).

problems.title: Full management chain with a recursive CTE
problems.question: employees(emp_id, name, manager_id). For every employee, list their full chain up to the CEO as a path string and their depth. What if the data contains a cycle?
problems.answer:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  -- anchor: the top (no manager)
  SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id,
         1 AS depth,
         name::VARCHAR AS path
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  -- recursive step: attach direct reports
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, e.manager_id,
         c.depth + 1,
         c.path || ' > ' || e.name
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.emp_id
  WHERE c.depth < 20                      -- guard rail
)
SELECT * FROM chain ORDER BY path;
  • Cycles (A manages B, B manages A) would recurse until the engine errors out. Guards: a depth limit as above, or carry an array of visited ids and stop when ARRAY_CONTAINS(e.emp_id::VARIANT, visited).
  • Employees whose chain never reaches a top-level manager (orphans) won't appear — run an anti-join check as a data-quality test.
  • Snowflake also has CONNECT BY with SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH and LEVEL (Oracle-style).
  • For BI, flatten to a bridge/closure table (ancestor_id, descendant_id, depth) once in dbt so analysts don't write recursion.
problems.lookfor: Anchor + recursive member, UNION ALL, cycle protection, and the modelling answer (closure table).
problems.followup: Total salary cost of each manager's entire organisation (sum over the closure table by ancestor).

problems.title: Pivot and unpivot
problems.question: sales(region, quarter, amount) with quarters Q1–Q4. Produce one row per region with columns Q1..Q4. Then reverse it.
problems.answer:
-- Conditional aggregation: portable, handles NULL/0 explicitly
SELECT region,
       SUM(IFF(quarter = 'Q1', amount, 0)) AS q1,
       SUM(IFF(quarter = 'Q2', amount, 0)) AS q2,
       SUM(IFF(quarter = 'Q3', amount, 0)) AS q3,
       SUM(IFF(quarter = 'Q4', amount, 0)) AS q4
FROM sales
GROUP BY region;

-- Snowflake PIVOT
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT region, quarter, amount FROM sales)
PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR quarter IN ('Q1','Q2','Q3','Q4')) AS p;
-- Snowflake also supports dynamic: FOR quarter IN (ANY ORDER BY quarter)

-- UNPIVOT back to rows
SELECT region, quarter, amount
FROM wide_sales
UNPIVOT (amount FOR quarter IN (q1, q2, q3, q4));

Notes: PIVOT returns NULL (not 0) for missing combinations; UNPIVOT drops NULLs by default (Snowflake has INCLUDE NULLS). Pivot only the columns you need in the inner query — extra columns become implicit grouping columns.
problems.lookfor: Both techniques, NULL behaviour, and the implicit-grouping gotcha.
problems.followup: Pivot when the list of values isn't known in advance (dynamic ANY, or generate SQL with a dbt macro such as dbt_utils.pivot).

problems.title: SCD Type 2 with MERGE
problems.question: dim_customer(customer_sk, customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to, is_current). A daily staging table stg_customer(customer_id, city, updated_at) arrives. Implement SCD Type 2: close the old version when city changes and insert the new version — in SQL, without dbt snapshots.
problems.answer:
The difficulty: one MERGE can only do one action per target row, but a change needs two actions (update the old row and insert the new one). The standard trick is to feed changed keys into the merge twice.

MERGE INTO dim_customer t
USING (
  -- rows whose key matches: used to CLOSE the current version
  SELECT s.customer_id AS merge_key, s.*
  FROM stg_customer s
  UNION ALL
  -- changed rows again with a NULL key: forces an INSERT of the new version
  SELECT NULL AS merge_key, s.*
  FROM stg_customer s
  JOIN dim_customer d
    ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id AND d.is_current
  WHERE d.city IS DISTINCT FROM s.city
) src
ON t.customer_id = src.merge_key AND t.is_current
WHEN MATCHED AND t.city IS DISTINCT FROM src.city THEN
  UPDATE SET valid_to = src.updated_at, is_current = FALSE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
  VALUES (src.customer_id, src.city, src.updated_at, NULL, TRUE);
  • Brand-new customers: their merge_key doesn't match → inserted by the first branch of the UNION.
  • Changed customers: first branch closes the old row; second branch (NULL key, never matches) inserts the new one.
  • Unchanged: matched but the AND condition fails → nothing.

Must-mention production points:

  • Dedupe staging first (one row per key per batch), or the MERGE is non-deterministic.
  • Use IS DISTINCT FROM (NULL-safe), or compare a hash of all tracked columns.
  • valid_to = NULL vs '9999-12-31': the far-future date makes BETWEEN joins simpler.
  • Late-arriving / out-of-order updates break simple SCD2 — need re-sequencing.
  • In dbt, this is snapshot (timestamp or check strategy).
problems.lookfor: The two-actions-per-row problem and the union trick (or a two-statement transaction: UPDATE then INSERT), dedup, NULL-safe comparison.
problems.followup: How do you handle hard deletes in the source? (Compare full source key set; close rows for missing keys; dbt snapshots have hard_deletes: invalidate | new_record.)

problems.title: Merge overlapping date ranges
problems.question: bookings(room_id, start_date, end_date). Bookings may overlap. Merge overlapping or touching ranges per room into continuous occupied periods.
problems.answer:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT room_id, start_date, end_date,
         MAX(end_date) OVER (PARTITION BY room_id ORDER BY start_date, end_date
                             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)
           AS max_prev_end
  FROM bookings
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT *,
         CASE WHEN max_prev_end IS NULL
                OR start_date > DATEADD(day, 1, max_prev_end)   -- gap → new period
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new
  FROM ordered
),
grouped AS (
  SELECT *, SUM(is_new) OVER (PARTITION BY room_id ORDER BY start_date, end_date
                              ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS grp
  FROM flagged
)
SELECT room_id, MIN(start_date) AS period_start, MAX(end_date) AS period_end
FROM grouped
GROUP BY room_id, grp
ORDER BY room_id, period_start;

Key insight: compare each start with the maximum end so far, not just the previous row's end. Example: [1–10], [2–3], [5–6] — row 3 starts after row 2 ends but is still inside row 1's range. Using LAG(end_date) gets this wrong.

"Touching" (end Mar 3, start Mar 4) counts as continuous here because of the +1 day; drop it if touching ranges should stay separate.
problems.lookfor: Running MAX instead of LAG, and clarifying touching vs overlapping.
problems.followup: Find double-bookings (pairs that overlap): self-join on a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end AND a.id < b.id.

problems.title: Monthly cohort retention table
problems.question: activity(user_id, activity_date). Build a retention table: for each signup-month cohort, the % of users active in month 0, 1, 2, … after their first month.
problems.answer:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC(month, MIN(activity_date)) AS cohort_month
  FROM activity GROUP BY user_id
),
active AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT a.user_id, f.cohort_month,
         DATEDIFF(month, f.cohort_month, DATE_TRUNC(month, a.activity_date)) AS month_n
  FROM activity a JOIN firsts f USING (user_id)
),
sizes AS (
  SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size FROM firsts GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT a.cohort_month, s.cohort_size, a.month_n,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)                              AS active_users,
       ROUND(100 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) / s.cohort_size, 1) AS retention_pct
FROM active a JOIN sizes s USING (cohort_month)
GROUP BY a.cohort_month, s.cohort_size, a.month_n
ORDER BY a.cohort_month, a.month_n;

Then pivot month_n into columns for the classic triangle (or let the BI tool do it).

Discussion: here DATEDIFF(month, …) on two month-truncated dates is exactly right (boundary counting is what we want). Define "active" with the business; recent cohorts have fewer observable months (the triangle shape) — don't average across cohorts naively. In dbt, materialise firsts as a user dimension.
problems.lookfor: Correct cohort definition, denominators from the cohort (not from active users), awareness of the right-censoring triangle.
problems.followup: Revenue retention instead of user retention (sum revenue per cohort per month ÷ month-0 revenue).

problems.title: Latest record per key — and the LAST_VALUE trap
problems.question: prices(product_id, price, effective_ts). Return the current price per product. Show three ways and explain why LAST_VALUE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY effective_ts) returns wrong results.
problems.answer:
-- 1. QUALIFY + ROW_NUMBER (most common)
SELECT product_id, price, effective_ts
FROM prices
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY effective_ts DESC) = 1;

-- 2. MAX_BY (Snowflake): concise, single aggregate
SELECT product_id, MAX_BY(price, effective_ts) AS current_price
FROM prices GROUP BY product_id;

-- 3. FIRST_VALUE with DESC order (no frame trap for FIRST_VALUE)
SELECT DISTINCT product_id,
       FIRST_VALUE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY effective_ts DESC) AS current_price
FROM prices;

Why LAST_VALUE "fails": with ORDER BY and no frame, the frame ends at the current row, so the "last value" is the current row's own price. Fix: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

Price "as of" a date (point-in-time join), very common in finance:

SELECT o.order_id, p.price
FROM orders o
ASOF JOIN prices p
  MATCH_CONDITION (o.order_ts >= p.effective_ts)
  ON o.product_id = p.product_id;

(ASOF JOIN exists in Snowflake; otherwise use a range join on valid_from/valid_to.)
problems.lookfor: Knowing frames, MAX_BY/MIN_BY, and point-in-time correctness.
problems.followup: Products whose price changed more than 3 times in 30 days (COUNT(*) with a range filter, or LAG + change flag).

problems.title: Percent of total and cumulative share
problems.question: For each product show revenue, its % of total revenue, and the cumulative % when sorted from highest revenue (Pareto/80-20 analysis).
problems.answer:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT product_id, revenue,
       ROUND(100 * RATIO_TO_REPORT(revenue) OVER (), 2)              AS pct_of_total,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id
                                      ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
                 / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 2)                           AS cumulative_pct
FROM rev
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

SUM(x) OVER () — an empty OVER() — is the grand total on every row. RATIO_TO_REPORT is Snowflake shorthand for x / SUM(x) OVER (). Products with cumulative_pct <= 80 are your "top 80%" set.
problems.lookfor: Empty OVER(), aggregating before windowing, deterministic ordering for the cumulative sum.
problems.followup: % of total within each category (OVER (PARTITION BY category)).

problems.title: Subtotals with GROUPING SETS / ROLLUP
problems.question: Produce revenue by (region, country), plus a subtotal per region and a grand total — in one query. How do you tell a subtotal row from a row where country is genuinely NULL?
problems.answer:
SELECT region,
       country,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue,
       GROUPING(country) AS is_country_subtotal,   -- 1 = this row aggregates all countries
       GROUPING(region)  AS is_grand_total
FROM sales
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, country)
ORDER BY region NULLS LAST, country NULLS LAST;
  • ROLLUP(a, b) = grouping sets (a,b), (a), () — hierarchical subtotals.
  • CUBE(a, b) = all combinations: (a,b), (a), (b), ().
  • GROUPING SETS ((a,b), (b)) = exactly the ones you list.
  • GROUPING(col) returns 1 when the NULL is a subtotal placeholder, 0 when it's real data — that's the answer to the second question. Label rows with IFF(GROUPING(country)=1, 'All countries', country).
problems.lookfor: Knowing all three, and GROUPING() to distinguish placeholder NULLs.
problems.followup: Why might a BI tool prefer you not to precompute subtotals in the warehouse? (Non-additive measures like distinct counts or averages can't be re-aggregated from subtotals.)

problems.title: Revenue doubled after a join (fan-out)
problems.question:
orders(order_id, customer_id, amount), order_items(order_id, sku), payments(order_id, paid_amount). An analyst writes:

SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue, SUM(p.paid_amount) AS paid
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN payments p   ON p.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;

Revenue is 3–6× too high. Explain and fix.
problems.answer:
Fan-out. An order with 3 items and 2 payments produces 3 × 2 = 6 joined rows, so o.amount is summed 6 times and each payment 3 times. Joining two independent one-to-many children to the same parent multiplies rows (a "chasm trap").

Fix: aggregate each child to the parent's grain before joining.

WITH items AS (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS item_count FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
),
pay AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(paid_amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.customer_id,
       SUM(o.amount)              AS revenue,
       SUM(COALESCE(p.paid, 0))   AS paid,
       SUM(COALESCE(i.item_count, 0)) AS items
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN pay   p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;

SUM(DISTINCT o.amount) is not a fix — two different orders with the same amount would be collapsed.

Prevention as an architect: document the grain of every model, add a unique test on the grain key in dbt, and add row-count reconciliation tests between layers.
problems.lookfor: Naming the grain problem, pre-aggregation, rejecting SUM(DISTINCT), and prevention through tests.
problems.followup: How would you detect fan-out automatically in a dbt project? (Unique tests on primary keys; dbt_utils.equal_rowcount/fewer_rows_than; compare COUNT(*) before and after joins in an audit query.)

problems.title: Capture COPY INTO load errors into an error_log table
problems.question: You load CSV files from a stage with COPY INTO. Bad rows must not stop the load, and every rejected row must be saved to an error_log table for the support team. How do you do it?
problems.answer:
A commonly given answer is:

-- ❌ does not work
INSERT INTO error_log
SELECT * FROM TABLE(VALIDATE(
  LOCATION => '@my_external_stage', VALIDATION_MODE => 'RETURN_ALL_ERRORS',
  TABLE_NAME => 'my_table', FILE_FORMAT => (TYPE => 'CSV')));

That mixes up two different features. VALIDATE is a table function that inspects a past COPY execution, and its only arguments are the target table and a JOB_ID. VALIDATION_MODE and FILE_FORMAT are options of COPY INTO itself.

Pattern 1 — load, skip bad rows, then log them (most common in production):

COPY INTO my_table
FROM @my_external_stage/orders/
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = csv_fmt)
ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';                 -- load good rows, skip bad ones

INSERT INTO error_log (logged_at, target_table, error, file, line, column_name, rejected_record)
SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), 'MY_TABLE', error, file, line, column_name, rejected_record
FROM TABLE(VALIDATE(my_table, JOB_ID => '_last'));

'_last' means the last COPY run in the current session. In an orchestrated job it's safer to capture the query id (LAST_QUERY_ID() right after the COPY, or from the orchestrator) and pass JOB_ID => '<query_id>'.

Pattern 2 — dry run before loading anything:

COPY INTO my_table FROM @my_external_stage/orders/
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = csv_fmt)
VALIDATION_MODE = 'RETURN_ERRORS';      -- loads nothing, returns errors

INSERT INTO error_log
SELECT * FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID()));

Limitations to mention:

  • VALIDATE and VALIDATION_MODE don't work with COPY statements that transform data (COPY INTO t FROM (SELECT $1, $2 … FROM @stage)). Workaround: load raw into a landing table with all-VARCHAR columns, then validate with TRY_CAST/TRY_TO_NUMBER in SQL and route failures to the error table.
  • For Snowpipe, use VALIDATE_PIPE_LOAD (last 14 days) and COPY_HISTORY.
  • ON_ERROR options: ABORT_STATEMENT (COPY default), CONTINUE, SKIP_FILE (Snowpipe default), SKIP_FILE_<n>, SKIP_FILE_<n>%.
problems.lookfor: Knowing VALIDATE vs VALIDATION_MODE, the _last session caveat, transformation limits, and a robust landing-table design.
problems.followup: Alert when more than 1% of rows in a file are rejected. (COPY_HISTORY gives ROW_COUNT and ERROR_COUNT per file; a task or Airflow check compares them.)

problems.title: Why didn't COPY reload my file? Load metadata explained
problems.question: A vendor re-sent orders_2026-11-01.csv with corrections, same file name. You run COPY INTO again and it reports "0 files processed". Why? How do you reload it safely?
problems.answer:
Snowflake keeps load metadata per table: which files (by path + ETag/checksum) were loaded, for 64 days. COPY skips files it has already loaded. This is what makes repeated COPY runs idempotent.

Here the file name is the same; whether it's skipped depends on whether its content checksum changed — if the vendor overwrote it with identical bytes, or metadata says it's loaded, it's skipped.

Options:

-- Force reload (beware: duplicates unless you delete first)
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE _source_file = 'orders_2026-11-01.csv';
COPY INTO orders FROM @stage/orders_2026-11-01.csv FORCE = TRUE;
COMMIT;
  • FORCE = TRUE loads regardless of metadata → duplicates unless you remove the previous rows. Keep METADATA$FILENAME in a _source_file column (or use INCLUDE_METADATA) so you can delete by file.
  • LOAD_UNCERTAIN_FILES = TRUE — for files older than 64 days whose status Snowflake can no longer determine.
  • Snowpipe keeps its own metadata for 14 days and won't reload a file with the same name; ALTER PIPE … REFRESH only queues files staged in the last 7 days.
  • Better design: vendors send new files with new names (versioned/timestamped), and the pipeline handles corrections via MERGE on business keys.
problems.lookfor: Load metadata, 64 vs 14 days, FORCE causing duplicates, and file-name lineage columns.
problems.followup: How would you make the whole load idempotent end-to-end? (Land raw with file name + row number, dedupe on business key, MERGE into the target.)

problems.title: Snowflake's architecture in three layers
problems.question: Explain Snowflake's architecture and why separating storage and compute matters. What runs in the cloud services layer?
problems.answer:
1. Storage layer — tables stored in the cloud provider's object storage as immutable, compressed, columnar micro-partitions. You pay per TB per month. Fully managed.
  2. Compute layer — virtual warehouses (MPP clusters). Each warehouse is independent: its own CPU, memory and local SSD cache. They all read the same storage.
  3. Cloud services layer — the "brain": authentication, access control, query parsing and optimisation, metadata (partition min/max stats, which enables pruning), transactions, result cache, infrastructure management.

Why separation matters:

  • Workload isolation: ELT on one warehouse, BI on another — no contention.
  • Elasticity: resize or add clusters in seconds; suspend when idle (per-second billing, 60-second minimum each time a warehouse starts).
  • Concurrency: multi-cluster warehouses scale out for many users.
  • Zero-copy features: cloning, Time Travel and sharing work by pointing at the same micro-partitions.

Cloud services usage is free up to 10% of daily warehouse compute; above that it's billed (watch for very high query counts, e.g. thousands of tiny queries or heavy metadata calls).
problems.lookfor: Accurate role of each layer, metadata-driven pruning, and the business benefits (isolation, elasticity, cost).
problems.followup: What does Snowflake's "hybrid of shared-disk and shared-nothing" mean? (Shared data in central storage like shared-disk; each warehouse processes in MPP shared-nothing style with local caching.)

problems.title: Micro-partitions and pruning — why isn't my query pruning?
problems.question: A 5 TB events table is queried with WHERE event_date = '2026-11-01'. The query profile shows "Partitions scanned: 41,000 of 42,000". Why so little pruning, and what can you do?
problems.answer:
Micro-partitions are 50–500 MB (uncompressed) immutable chunks. For each one, Snowflake stores per-column metadata: min/max, distinct count, null count. Pruning = skipping partitions whose min/max range can't match the filter.

Pruning fails when:

  1. Data isn't ordered by the filter column. If rows for every date are spread across all partitions (e.g. loaded by customer_id, or many late-arriving updates), every partition's min/max date range covers 2026-11-01.
  2. The filter wraps the column in a function: WHERE TO_DATE(event_ts) = … or WHERE DATE_TRUNC('day', event_ts) = … can prune poorly; prefer a range on the raw column: event_ts >= '2026-11-01' AND event_ts < '2026-11-02'.
  3. Implicit casts (comparing a VARCHAR column to a number).
  4. Join filters that aren't pushed down — Snowflake does join-based pruning in many cases, but filtering the fact table directly is more reliable.

Fixes, cheapest first:

  • Rewrite predicates to be prunable.
  • Load data in natural order (by date) — most append-only event tables are naturally clustered by ingestion time.
  • Add a clustering key on event_date (see clustering problem) if the table is large, filtered heavily, and rarely updated randomly.
  • Search optimization if the access pattern is needle-in-haystack lookups on a high-cardinality column.

Check: SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('events', '(event_date)'); → look at average_depth (lower is better) and overlap histogram.
problems.lookfor: Correct micro-partition facts, reading "partitions scanned vs total", and ordered remedies.
problems.followup: Why does a big UPDATE touching random rows hurt clustering? (Micro-partitions are immutable — updated rows are rewritten into new partitions, scattering ranges.)

problems.title: Choosing a clustering key
problems.question: When would you add a clustering key, how do you choose the columns, and what does it cost? When would you not do it?
problems.answer:
Add one when all are true:

  • Table is large (multi-TB; small tables don't benefit).
  • Queries filter (or join) on the same columns most of the time.
  • Pruning is poor today (SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION shows high average depth).
  • The table isn't constantly updated randomly — reclustering churn costs money.

Choosing columns:

  • Start with the most common filter — usually a date.
  • Order multi-column keys from lowest to highest cardinality (e.g. (event_date, region)).
  • Avoid very high-cardinality columns (timestamps, UUIDs) directly — use an expression: CLUSTER BY (TO_DATE(event_ts)) or (event_date, SUBSTR(customer_id, 1, 2)).
  • Keep it to 3–4 columns max.
ALTER TABLE events CLUSTER BY (event_date, region);
SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('events');
-- cost tracking
SELECT * FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.AUTOMATIC_CLUSTERING_HISTORY
WHERE table_name = 'EVENTS' ORDER BY start_time DESC;

Cost: Automatic Clustering runs serverless in the background, billed in credits, plus extra storage from rewritten partitions (old ones are kept for Time Travel/Fail-safe). The initial clustering of a big table can be expensive; estimate first with SYSTEM$ESTIMATE_AUTOMATIC_CLUSTERING_COSTS and suspend with ALTER TABLE … SUSPEND RECLUSTER if needed.

Don't cluster when: the table is small; queries filter on many different columns (consider search optimization, or materialised/dynamic tables with different sort orders); heavy random DML; or natural load order already gives good pruning.
problems.lookfor: Data-driven decision (measure before/after), cardinality ordering, cost awareness, alternatives.
problems.followup: How would you prove the clustering paid off? (Compare partitions scanned, query time and credits for the top queries before vs after, vs the clustering credits spent.)

problems.title: The three caches — and when the result cache is NOT used
problems.question: Explain Snowflake's caches. A dashboard runs the same query every 5 minutes but never hits the result cache. List the reasons.
problems.answer:
cache where lifetime notes
Result cache cloud services 24 h, extended on each reuse (up to 31 days) returns stored results; no warehouse needed
Warehouse (local disk) cache warehouse SSD until the warehouse suspends caches micro-partition data read from storage; "Percentage scanned from cache" in the profile
Metadata cache cloud services always answers COUNT(*), MIN/MAX on columns, etc. without a warehouse

The result cache is not used when:

  • Query text differs (even whitespace/case of literals, different parameter values).
  • Underlying data changed (any DML on the tables, even unrelated rows).
  • The query uses non-deterministic functions: CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), RANDOM(), UUID_STRING() — very common in dashboards ("last 7 days from now").
  • It references external tables, or certain functions (UDFs that aren't deterministic, some system functions).
  • USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE in the session.
  • Role lacks privileges on the objects (each role must be authorised).
  • Result older than its retention.

Fix for the dashboard: compute the date boundary as CURRENT_DATE truncated (deterministic within a day isn't guaranteed either — better: let the BI tool pass a fixed date literal), or serve it from a pre-aggregated table refreshed on a schedule.

Auto-suspend trade-off: a short suspend (60 s) saves credits but drops the warehouse cache; BI warehouses often use 5–10 minutes.
problems.lookfor: All three caches, the full list of result-cache blockers, and the auto-suspend trade-off.
problems.followup: Does the result cache cost anything? (No warehouse credits; just cloud services, which is usually within the free 10%.)

problems.title: Time Travel, Fail-safe and table types — including the dbt surprise
problems.question: Explain Time Travel and Fail-safe, and the difference between permanent, transient and temporary tables. Then: a teammate dropped a dbt-built table in production — "no problem, Fail-safe has it". Are they right?
problems.answer:
• Time Travel: query or restore data as of a past time: SELECT … AT(OFFSET => -3600), BEFORE(STATEMENT => '<query_id>'), UNDROP TABLE, CREATE TABLE … CLONE … AT(…). Retention set by DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS: 0–1 day on Standard edition; up to 90 days for permanent objects on Enterprise and above.
  • Fail-safe: a further 7 days after Time Travel ends, for permanent tables only. Not user-accessible — recovery is via Snowflake Support, best-effort, for disasters.
type Time Travel Fail-safe lives
permanent 0–90 days (edition-dependent) 7 days until dropped
transient 0–1 day none until dropped
temporary 0–1 day none the session only

The dbt surprise: dbt-snowflake creates tables as transient by default (transient: true) to save storage cost. So the dropped table has at most 1 day of Time Travel and no Fail-safe. If more than a day passed, it's gone — rebuild it with dbt (fine for derived models, a disaster for anything that holds history, like snapshots or incremental models fed by sources that no longer have the data).

Good practice: set +transient: false for incremental models, snapshots and anything not fully rebuildable; and use longer retention on critical raw/landing tables.

Storage note: Time Travel and Fail-safe both store changed/deleted micro-partitions — high-churn tables with long retention can cost more in "time travel bytes" than in active bytes (TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS).
problems.lookfor: Precise numbers, the support-only nature of Fail-safe, and the dbt transient default — a strong practical signal.
problems.followup: How do you restore a table to how it was before a bad UPDATE at 10:15? (CREATE TABLE t_restored CLONE t BEFORE(STATEMENT => '<bad_query_id>'), verify, then ALTER TABLE … SWAP WITH.)

problems.title: Zero-copy cloning: how it works and what to watch for
problems.question: How does zero-copy cloning work, what does it cost, and how would you use it for dev/test environments? Any gotchas?
problems.answer:
A clone copies metadata only — the new object points to the same micro-partitions. No data is copied, so it's near-instant and costs nothing extra at creation. Storage is charged only for partitions that change after cloning (each side diverges independently).

CREATE DATABASE analytics_dev CLONE analytics_prod;
CREATE TABLE orders_backup CLONE orders AT(TIMESTAMP => '2026-11-20 09:00'::TIMESTAMP_LTZ);
CREATE SCHEMA ci_pr_1234 CLONE analytics_prod.marts;

Uses:

  • Dev/test environments with production-like data in seconds.
  • CI for dbt: clone prod, build only changed models into the clone (see slim CI problem).
  • Backups before risky migrations; point-in-time restore combined with Time Travel.

Gotchas:

  • Grants: a cloned table doesn't keep the source table's grants unless you use COPY GRANTS; when cloning a database/schema, child objects keep their grants but the container itself doesn't.
  • Tasks in a cloned database/schema are suspended — good, otherwise your dev clone would start writing data.
  • Pipes and stages have special rules (e.g. pipes pointing at internal stages aren't cloned) — check before relying on them.
  • PII: a prod clone in dev exposes production data. Apply masking policies (they travel with the objects) or build a masked copy.
  • Long-lived clones diverge and accumulate their own storage — schedule cleanup.
  • Clones are separate objects: later changes to prod don't flow into the clone.
problems.lookfor: Metadata-pointer explanation, cost model, CI use, grants/tasks/PII gotchas.
problems.followup: How is cloning different from data sharing? (Clone = new independent object in your account; share = read-only live access for another account, no copy.)

problems.title: Streams: how CDC works inside Snowflake
problems.question: How does a Snowflake stream work? What are the stream types? What makes a stream "stale", and how do two different pipelines consume the same table's changes?
problems.answer:
A stream is an offset (a bookmark in the table's version history) plus change-tracking metadata. Querying it returns rows changed since the offset, with extra columns:

  • METADATA$ACTION — INSERT or DELETE
  • METADATA$ISUPDATE — TRUE when the insert/delete pair represents an update
  • METADATA$ROW_ID — stable row identifier
CREATE STREAM orders_stream ON TABLE raw.orders;   -- standard (delta) stream

MERGE INTO core.orders t
USING (SELECT * FROM orders_stream WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT') s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET …
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT …;     -- offset advances when this DML commits

Types:

  • Standard: inserts, updates, deletes (net changes).
  • Append-only: inserts only — cheaper, ideal for append-only raw tables.
  • Insert-only: for external tables / some Iceberg tables.

Key behaviours:

  • The offset advances only when the stream is consumed in a DML statement that commits. A plain SELECT doesn't advance it. Wrap multi-statement consumption in an explicit transaction so all statements see the same changes.
  • Net changes: a row inserted then deleted between consumptions doesn't appear.
  • Staleness: a stream relies on the table's Time Travel history. If it isn't consumed within the retention period, Snowflake extends retention for the stream up to MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS (default 14 days); beyond that the stream becomes stale and must be recreated (with a full reload). Monitor STALE_AFTER in SHOW STREAMS.
  • Multiple consumers: create one stream per consumer. If two pipelines read one stream, the first to commit advances the offset and the second misses the changes.
  • SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('orders_stream') — used in task WHEN clauses to skip empty runs.
problems.lookfor: Offset semantics, when the offset moves, staleness, one stream per consumer.
problems.followup: Stream vs dynamic table for the same job? (Streams + tasks = full control, procedural; dynamic tables = declarative, Snowflake manages refresh — see that problem.)

problems.title: Tasks and task graphs
problems.question: Design a Snowflake-native pipeline: every 5 minutes, process new rows from a stream through three dependent steps, skip runs when there's no data, and alert on failure. How do tasks work?
problems.answer:
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK t_root
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh                 -- or omit for serverless tasks
  SCHEDULE  = '5 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('raw_orders_stream')
AS
  CALL load_staging();

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK t_transform
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  AFTER t_root
AS
  CALL build_core();

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK t_publish
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  AFTER t_transform
AS
  CALL refresh_marts();

-- tasks are created SUSPENDED; resume children first, root last
ALTER TASK t_publish RESUME;
ALTER TASK t_transform RESUME;
ALTER TASK t_root RESUME;
-- or: SELECT SYSTEM$TASK_DEPENDENTS_ENABLE('t_root');

Points:

  • Task graph (DAG): only the root has a schedule; children use AFTER. A task can have multiple predecessors.
  • WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA is evaluated in cloud services — if false, the run is skipped and no warehouse starts.
  • Serverless vs warehouse: serverless tasks size themselves and are billed per use — good for small frequent jobs; a shared warehouse can be cheaper for heavy batches.
  • Finalizer task (FINALIZE = t_root) runs after the graph completes, success or failure — for cleanup and notifications.
  • Failure handling: SUSPEND_TASK_AFTER_NUM_FAILURES, TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS, ERROR_INTEGRATION to push failure notifications to SNS/Event Grid/Pub/Sub, and monitoring via TASK_HISTORY().
  • Overlap: by default a graph run won't start while the previous one is running (ALLOW_OVERLAPPING_EXECUTION = FALSE).
  • Tasks run as the task owner role — design grants accordingly.

When to use Airflow instead: cross-system dependencies (APIs, files, other platforms), complex retries/branching, SLAs across tools, one place to observe everything.
problems.lookfor: Root-only schedule, resume order, stream-gated runs, failure notifications, and a clear "tasks vs Airflow" view.
problems.followup: Tasks vs dynamic tables vs Airflow for a 10-step transformation? (Often: dynamic tables or dbt for the transformations, Airflow for cross-system orchestration, tasks for small in-Snowflake jobs.)

problems.title: Dynamic tables vs streams + tasks vs materialized views
problems.question: You need a continuously updated customer_360 table joining orders, payments and support tickets, fresh within 10 minutes. Compare dynamic tables, streams + tasks, and materialized views. Which do you pick?
problems.answer:
Dynamic table Streams + tasks Materialized view
style declarative (a SELECT) procedural (you write MERGE logic) declarative
joins / aggregations yes anything you code single table only, no joins, limited functions
freshness TARGET_LAG (e.g. '10 minutes' or DOWNSTREAM) your schedule always current (maintained in background)
incremental automatic where possible (REFRESH_MODE = AUTO/INCREMENTAL/FULL) you implement it automatic
compute your warehouse warehouse or serverless serverless
control less (can't DML into it) total little 
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE customer_360
  TARGET_LAG = '10 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE  = transform_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = AUTO
AS
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
       SUM(p.amount)              AS paid,
       COUNT(DISTINCT t.ticket_id) AS tickets
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders   o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id    = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN tickets  t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY 1, 2;

(Note the fan-out risk in this exact query — payments and tickets both multiply rows; pre-aggregate each child in its own dynamic table first.)

My choice here: dynamic tables — joins + aggregation, a freshness SLA, minimal code, built-in lineage and refresh history. Chain them (TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM for intermediate tables).

Watch-outs for dynamic tables:

  • Some constructs force full refresh (non-deterministic functions, certain window/outer-join patterns) — check REFRESH_MODE and refresh_mode_reason after creating.
  • Base tables need change tracking (enabled automatically if you own them).
  • CREATE OR REPLACE on an upstream base table breaks incremental refresh (new object) — use INSERT OVERWRITE or MERGE upstream.
  • Cost is driven by the target lag: 1 minute lag on a large join can burn a warehouse continuously.

Pick streams + tasks for complex procedural logic (SCD2 with custom rules, deletes propagation, calling external functions), and materialized views for simple single-table aggregates/projections that need to be always current, e.g. a re-clustered projection of a huge table.

dbt supports materialized='dynamic_table' on Snowflake.
problems.lookfor: Accurate MV limits, TARGET_LAG/refresh mode knowledge, cost thinking, and catching the fan-out.
problems.followup: How do you monitor dynamic table freshness? (DYNAMIC_TABLE_REFRESH_HISTORY, lag metrics in Snowsight, alert if actual lag exceeds target.)

problems.title: COPY vs Snowpipe vs Snowpipe Streaming
problems.question: Files land in S3 continuously, and a Kafka topic produces events. Which ingestion method for each? Explain the costs and file-size guidance.
problems.answer:
COPY INTO (batch) Snowpipe Snowpipe Streaming
unit files files rows (no files)
trigger you/orchestrator cloud event notification (auto-ingest) or REST client SDK / Kafka connector
latency minutes–hours ~1 minute typical seconds
compute your warehouse serverless serverless
load metadata 64 days 14 days n/a (offset tokens)
  • S3 files continuously → Snowpipe with AUTO_INGEST = TRUE (S3 event → SQS → pipe). No warehouse to manage.
  • Kafka → Snowpipe Streaming (Kafka connector in streaming mode), landing rows directly with low latency. Exactly-once is handled via channels and offset tokens.
  • Large daily/hourly batches → COPY on a warehouse you size for the job.

File sizing (for COPY and Snowpipe): aim for roughly 100–250 MB compressed per file. Thousands of tiny files add per-file overhead (ingestion cost and latency) and slow listing; a single 50 GB file can't be parallelised well — split it.

Other points: Snowpipe has no guaranteed order across files; dedupe downstream. Pipes can be paused (ALTER PIPE … SET PIPE_EXECUTION_PAUSED = TRUE) for maintenance. Monitor with COPY_HISTORY, PIPE_USAGE_HISTORY, SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS.

Also worth knowing: Openflow (Snowflake's managed integration service based on Apache NiFi) for connector-based ingestion from databases and SaaS sources.
problems.lookfor: Matching the method to latency and format, file sizing, and monitoring.
problems.followup: How do you handle schema changes in Snowpipe loads? (Land as VARIANT or with MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME; table schema evolution with ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION = TRUE.)

problems.title: Warehouse sizing: scale up or scale out?
problems.question: Two complaints: (1) the nightly transformation job is slow; (2) at 9 am, BI dashboards are slow because queries queue. What do you do for each?
problems.answer:
• Scale UP (bigger size) for complex/large queries — more CPU, memory and local disk per query. Each size up doubles credits per hour and roughly halves run time for well-parallelised queries, so cost can stay similar while time drops. Clear signal: spilling to local/remote storage in the query profile.
  • Scale OUT (multi-cluster) for concurrency — more clusters of the same size when many queries run at once. Signal: queued time (QUEUED_OVERLOAD_TIME in query history). Requires Enterprise edition.

So: (1) nightly job → bigger warehouse for that job (or split into parallel steps); (2) BI → multi-cluster warehouse:

ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET
  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
  MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 4
  SCALING_POLICY    = 'STANDARD'   -- start clusters quickly; 'ECONOMY' waits for sustained load
  AUTO_SUSPEND      = 300
  AUTO_RESUME       = TRUE;

More levers:

  • Separate warehouses per workload (ELT, BI, data science, ad hoc) for isolation and cost attribution.
  • STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS and STATEMENT_QUEUED_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS as guard rails.
  • MAX_CONCURRENCY_LEVEL controls how many queries a cluster runs at once.
  • Snowpark-optimized warehouses for memory-heavy Python/ML work.
  • Query Acceleration Service for occasional scan-heavy outliers rather than upsizing for everyone.
  • Billing: per second with a 60-second minimum each time a warehouse resumes — very frequent suspend/resume of tiny jobs wastes credits.
problems.lookfor: Correct diagnosis signals (spill vs queue), multi-cluster settings, workload isolation.
problems.followup: How would you right-size every warehouse in the account? (Query history: execution time, spill, queue, utilisation per warehouse; try one size down/up and compare cost × time.)

problems.title: Diagnose a slow query with the Query Profile
problems.question: A query that used to take 2 minutes now takes 40. Walk through how you'd diagnose it in Snowflake and the most common root causes with fixes.
problems.answer:
Step 1 — Is it the query or the environment? Query history: compare QUEUED_OVERLOAD_TIME, QUEUED_PROVISIONING_TIME, COMPILATION_TIME, EXECUTION_TIME, warehouse size, and bytes scanned vs the fast runs. Queuing = concurrency problem, not query problem.

Step 2 — Query Profile. Look at "Most expensive nodes" and the statistics panel:

symptom in profile likely cause fix
Partitions scanned ≈ total no pruning prunable predicates, clustering, filter earlier
Bytes spilled to local/remote storage not enough memory bigger warehouse, reduce data earlier, avoid huge sorts/DISTINCT
Join output rows ≫ input rows exploding join (duplicate keys, missing join condition) fix join keys, dedupe, check grain
Big "Aggregate" or "Sort" huge GROUP BY / ORDER BY pre-aggregate, remove unnecessary ORDER BY
Large "TableScan" of a view repeated complex view used multiple times materialise intermediate results
UNION instead of UNION ALL unnecessary dedup sort use UNION ALL
High remote disk I/O, low cache % cold warehouse cache expected after resume; consider auto-suspend settings

Step 3 — What changed? Data volume growth, a new join, stats of skew (one key with millions of rows), a view definition change, clustering degraded after a backfill, warehouse resized, a changed dbt model.

Common rewrites: filter before joining; select only needed columns (columnar storage — SELECT * reads everything); replace correlated logic with window functions; QUALIFY instead of self-joins; avoid functions on join keys; break mega-queries into staged temp tables.

Tooling: GET_QUERY_OPERATOR_STATS(<query_id>) returns profile stats as rows — useful to automate regression checks.
problems.lookfor: A structured method (environment → profile → change), reading spill/pruning/explosion correctly.
problems.followup: How would you catch performance regressions before production? (Run key queries in CI against a clone, compare bytes_scanned/time, alert on >X% increase.)

problems.title: Controlling and attributing Snowflake cost
problems.question: Finance asks: "What does each team spend on Snowflake, and how do we stop surprise bills?" Design the cost controls.
problems.answer:
Visibility (attribution):

  • Separate warehouses per team/workload → WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY gives credits per warehouse.
  • Shared warehouses → QUERY_TAG set per job/team (ALTER SESSION SET QUERY_TAG = 'team=finance;job=daily_pnl', dbt query_tag config) and QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY for per-query compute cost.
  • Object tags (cost_center) on warehouses/databases for chargeback reports.
  • Don't forget non-warehouse costs: storage (TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS), serverless features (Snowpipe, clustering, search optimization, tasks, dynamic tables), cloud services above 10%, data transfer, AI functions. METERING_DAILY_HISTORY covers them.

Controls:

  • Resource monitors on warehouses: credit quota per day/month with NOTIFY at 75%, SUSPEND at 100%, SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE at 110%. Limitation: they only cover warehouse credits, not serverless features.
  • Budgets cover serverless features and custom groups of objects with alerts.
  • Auto-suspend on every warehouse (60–300 s), auto-resume on.
  • STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS per warehouse to kill runaway queries.
  • Restrict who can create or resize warehouses (only via Terraform/platform team).
CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR finance_rm WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 500
  FREQUENCY = MONTHLY START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
           ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND
           ON 110 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE;
ALTER WAREHOUSE finance_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = finance_rm;

Culture: a weekly cost report by team, top 20 most expensive queries with owners, and a cost check in code review for new dbt models.
problems.lookfor: Attribution and control as separate topics, knowing resource monitors don't cover serverless, query tags.
problems.followup: Top 10 most expensive queries last week, with user and warehouse — write the query on QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY joined to QUERY_HISTORY.

problems.title: Search Optimization vs clustering vs Query Acceleration
problems.question: Three workloads: (a) support agents look up a single customer by email in a 3 billion-row table; (b) analysts filter by date range on the same table; (c) a few ad-hoc queries occasionally scan huge amounts of data. Which feature for each?
problems.answer:
• (a) Search Optimization Service (SOS) — builds a persistent search access path for highly selective point lookups: equality / IN on high-cardinality columns, substring and regex (LIKE '%x%'), fields inside VARIANT, geospatial. Clustering can't help a needle-in-a-haystack email lookup.
ALTER TABLE customers_events ADD SEARCH OPTIMIZATION ON EQUALITY(email), SUBSTRING(email);
SELECT SYSTEM$ESTIMATE_SEARCH_OPTIMIZATION_COSTS('customers_events', 'EQUALITY(email)');
  • (b) Clustering key on the date — range filters on a low/medium-cardinality column, many rows returned.
  • (c) Query Acceleration Service (QAS) — offloads portions of eligible large scans/filters to shared serverless compute, so an outlier query doesn't force you to upsize the whole warehouse.
ALTER WAREHOUSE adhoc_wh SET ENABLE_QUERY_ACCELERATION = TRUE
                            QUERY_ACCELERATION_MAX_SCALE_FACTOR = 8;
SELECT SYSTEM$ESTIMATE_QUERY_ACCELERATION('<query_id>');

Costs: SOS = serverless build/maintenance credits + extra storage (more on high-churn tables); clustering = serverless reclustering; QAS = serverless credits per accelerated query. All are Enterprise-edition features.

Rule of thumb: SOS for "find these few rows", clustering for "scan this slice", QAS for "occasional huge scan", bigger warehouse for "complex compute/spill".
problems.lookfor: Matching access pattern to feature, and cost awareness.
problems.followup: How do you check if a query actually used search optimization? (Query profile shows "Search Optimization Access" and partitions pruned by it.)

problems.title: Querying nested JSON with VARIANT and FLATTEN
problems.question: raw_orders(payload VARIANT) holds JSON like: {"order_id": 7, "customer": {"id": 42, "tier": "gold"}, "items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "B9", "qty": 1}]} Produce one row per item with order_id, customer id, sku and qty. Orders with an empty items array must still appear.
problems.answer:
SELECT
  r.payload:order_id::NUMBER          AS order_id,
  r.payload:customer.id::NUMBER       AS customer_id,
  r.payload:customer.tier::STRING     AS tier,
  i.value:sku::STRING                 AS sku,
  i.value:qty::NUMBER                 AS qty,
  i.index                             AS item_position
FROM raw_orders r,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(INPUT => r.payload:items, OUTER => TRUE) i;

Key points:

  • : navigates JSON, . goes deeper, [0] indexes arrays; always cast (::STRING) — otherwise you get VARIANT values with quotes.
  • JSON keys are case-sensitive.
  • FLATTEN returns SEQ, KEY, PATH, INDEX, VALUE, THIS. OUTER => TRUE keeps rows whose array is empty/missing (like a LEFT JOIN) — the requirement here.
  • Nested arrays: chain FLATTENs (… , LATERAL FLATTEN(i.value:discounts) d). RECURSIVE => TRUE walks every level (useful for exploring unknown schemas).
  • Missing key → NULL; JSON null → VARIANT null (IS_NULL_VALUE() distinguishes them).
  • Performance: Snowflake extracts common JSON paths into columnar sub-columns automatically, so frequently used fields prune and scan efficiently. For heavily queried fields, still materialise typed columns in a staging model.
  • Loading: STRIP_OUTER_ARRAY = TRUE when a file contains one big JSON array.
problems.lookfor: Correct path syntax, casting, OUTER => TRUE, and the staging-model recommendation.
problems.followup: Build JSON back from rows: OBJECT_CONSTRUCT('sku', sku, 'qty', qty) and ARRAY_AGG(...) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …).

problems.title: Masking policies, row access policies and tag-based masking
problems.question: HR data: everyone may query employees, but only HR sees full salaries and national IDs; managers see only their own region's rows. How do you implement this in Snowflake without creating separate views per role?
problems.answer:
Column masking (dynamic data masking):

CREATE MASKING POLICY pii_mask AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING ->
  CASE WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('HR_PII_READER') THEN val
       ELSE '***MASKED***' END;

ALTER TABLE employees MODIFY COLUMN national_id SET MASKING POLICY pii_mask;

Row-level security (row access policy) with a mapping table:

CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY region_rap AS (region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
  IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('HR_ADMIN')
  OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM security.region_access m
             WHERE m.role_name = CURRENT_ROLE() AND m.region = region);

ALTER TABLE employees ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY region_rap ON (region);

Tag-based masking — scales to hundreds of tables:

CREATE TAG governance.pii_type ALLOWED_VALUES 'national_id','email','phone';
ALTER TAG governance.pii_type SET MASKING POLICY pii_mask;
ALTER TABLE employees MODIFY COLUMN national_id SET TAG governance.pii_type = 'national_id';
-- any column with this tag is masked automatically

Design points:

  • Use IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION() rather than CURRENT_ROLE() = … so role hierarchy and secondary roles work.
  • Policies are applied at query time, wherever the column is used (views, clones, shares) — one place to govern.
  • Policy mapping tables should be owned by a security role and kept small/fast.
  • Automatic data classification can suggest PII tags.
  • Audit with ACCESS_HISTORY (who read which columns) and POLICY_REFERENCES.
  • These features require Enterprise edition or higher.
  • Masking can break joins on masked columns — tokenise deterministically (e.g. SHA2(val)) if analysts must join on PII.
problems.lookfor: Both policy types, tag-based scaling, IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION, auditing.
problems.followup: How do you let analysts count distinct customers by email without seeing emails? (Mask to a deterministic hash.)

problems.title: Designing roles (RBAC) for a data platform
problems.question: Design the role model for a Snowflake account with raw, staging and mart layers, used by data engineers, analysts, a BI tool and dbt service accounts, across dev and prod.
problems.answer:
Principles: least privilege; grant privileges to roles, roles to users; never to users directly; separate access roles (what objects) from functional roles (who you are).

System roles:   ORGADMIN · ACCOUNTADMIN (break-glass, MFA, ≤3 people)
                SECURITYADMIN (grants) · USERADMIN (users/roles) · SYSADMIN (object owner tree)

Access roles (often database roles):
  PROD_RAW_R, PROD_RAW_RW, PROD_MARTS_R, PROD_MARTS_RW, DEV_ALL_RW …

Functional roles (granted to users/service accounts):
  DATA_ENGINEER   → PROD_RAW_R, PROD_MARTS_R, DEV_ALL_RW
  ANALYST         → PROD_MARTS_R
  BI_SERVICE      → PROD_MARTS_R
  DBT_PROD        → PROD_RAW_R, PROD_MARTS_RW  (owns mart objects)
  LOADER          → PROD_RAW_RW

All custom roles roll up to SYSADMIN so admins can manage objects.

Key mechanisms:

  • Future grants so new tables are readable automatically: GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA prod.marts TO ROLE prod_marts_r;
  • Managed access schemas — only the schema owner (or a role with MANAGE GRANTS) can grant on objects, preventing object owners from sharing ad hoc.
  • Database roles — access roles scoped inside a database; they travel with clones/replication and can be shared.
  • Warehouses: separate USAGE grants per functional role.
  • Service users: key-pair or OAuth authentication, TYPE = SERVICE, no passwords; network policies.
  • Ownership: the dbt prod role owns objects it creates; use COPY GRANTS / dbt grants config to keep grants stable across rebuilds.
  • Everything defined as code (Terraform or a permissions tool) and reviewed.
problems.lookfor: Access vs functional roles, future grants, managed access, service-account security, IaC.
problems.followup: A user has role A and B. How can they query objects from both in one query? (Secondary roles: USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL.)

problems.title: Secure Data Sharing
problems.question: A partner company wants daily access to a subset of your sales data. They also use Snowflake, but in a different cloud region. Another partner doesn't use Snowflake at all. How do you share with both?
problems.answer:
How sharing works: a share grants another account read-only access to your objects. No data is copied — the consumer queries your micro-partitions live, using their compute. Updates are visible immediately.

CREATE SHARE partner_sales;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sales TO SHARE partner_sales;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sales.shared TO SHARE partner_sales;
GRANT SELECT ON VIEW sales.shared.v_partner_sales TO SHARE partner_sales;  -- must be a SECURE view
ALTER SHARE partner_sales ADD ACCOUNTS = partnerorg.partneraccount;
-- consumer: CREATE DATABASE partner_data FROM SHARE provider_acct.partner_sales;
  • Share secure views (definition hidden, optimiser won't leak data) that filter to the partner's rows — e.g. using CURRENT_ACCOUNT() with a mapping table for multi-tenant shares.
  • Different region/cloud: direct shares work within a region. Across regions, replicate the database to an account in the partner's region, or publish a listing (private or Marketplace) with cross-cloud auto-fulfilment, which handles replication.
  • Non-Snowflake partner: a reader account — a Snowflake account you create and manage for them; you pay their compute. Control it with a resource monitor.
  • Governance: masking/row policies apply; consumers can't re-share; track usage with listing analytics.
  • Other options: data clean rooms when neither party should see raw rows; or unload files if they need extracts.
problems.lookfor: No-copy architecture, secure views, region limits, reader accounts and who pays.
problems.followup: How would you version a share so you can change table structures without breaking partners? (Share stable views as a contract; add v2 views; deprecate with notice.)

problems.title: MERGE fails with "Duplicate row detected"
problems.question: A MERGE into customers fails with "Duplicate row detected during DML action". What happened, and why is it dangerous to just switch the error off?
problems.answer:
The source has more than one row for the same join key, so one target row matches several source rows. Which source row should win is undefined → Snowflake raises an error because ERROR_ON_NONDETERMINISTIC_MERGE is TRUE by default (same idea for UPDATE with joins: ERROR_ON_NONDETERMINISTIC_UPDATE).

Setting it to FALSE makes Snowflake pick an arbitrary row — results can differ between runs: a silent data-quality bug.

Fix: deduplicate the source to the merge key with a deterministic rule.

MERGE INTO customers t
USING (
  SELECT *
  FROM stg_customers
  QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                             ORDER BY updated_at DESC, _loaded_at DESC) = 1
) s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
