WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET …   -- ignore older updates
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT …;

Also: WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at protects against out-of-order batches overwriting newer data. And handle deletes with WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_deleted THEN DELETE.
problems.lookfor: Root cause, refusing to disable the check, deterministic dedup and ordering guards.
problems.followup: In dbt with incremental_strategy='merge', where do you put this dedup? (In the model's SELECT, ideally with QUALIFY on the incremental slice.)

problems.title: Transactions, DDL and idempotent loads
problems.question: A load job runs: DELETE today's rows, CREATE TABLE tmp …, INSERT new rows. It sometimes fails halfway and leaves the table empty. Why, and how do you make it safe?
problems.answer:
In Snowflake DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP…) commit implicitly — they end the current transaction. So BEGIN; DELETE …; CREATE TABLE … commits the DELETE immediately; if the INSERT then fails, the deleted data is gone.

Safe patterns:

-- 1. Keep DDL outside the transaction
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_orders AS SELECT … ;   -- before BEGIN
BEGIN;
  DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_date = '2026-11-21';
  INSERT INTO orders SELECT * FROM tmp_orders;
COMMIT;

-- 2. Single atomic statement
MERGE INTO orders …;                       -- one statement = atomic
INSERT OVERWRITE INTO daily_summary SELECT …; -- replace contents atomically

-- 3. Build-and-swap
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE orders_new AS SELECT …;
ALTER TABLE orders SWAP WITH orders_new;    -- atomic metadata swap

Idempotency — running the job twice for the same date gives the same result:

  • Delete + insert scoped to the batch (date/partition), or MERGE on business keys.
  • Parameterise by logical date (from the orchestrator), never "now".
  • Record the batch id/run id in the rows.

Other facts: autocommit is on by default (each statement is its own transaction); a failed statement inside an explicit transaction doesn't automatically roll back the transaction; stored procedures can control transactions; Snowflake isolation is READ COMMITTED for tables.
problems.lookfor: Implicit DDL commit, atomic alternatives, and idempotency defined clearly.
problems.followup: How do you backfill 90 days safely with this pattern? (Loop over dates, each one idempotent; or INSERT OVERWRITE per partition range; run in parallel with limits.)

problems.title: ACCOUNT_USAGE vs INFORMATION_SCHEMA
problems.question: You need query history for a monitoring dashboard. Should you use SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY or INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY()? What's the difference?
problems.answer:
SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE INFORMATION_SCHEMA
scope whole account one database (plus table functions with limited scope)
latency delayed — roughly 45 minutes to 3 hours depending on view near real-time
retention 365 days short — e.g. 7 days of query history, 14 days of load/copy history
dropped objects included (with DELETED timestamps) not included
access needs IMPORTED PRIVILEGES on the SNOWFLAKE db (or specific database roles) your role's visible objects

For a monitoring dashboard with trends → ACCOUNT_USAGE (long history, account-wide). For real-time alerting ("is the job running now?", "did the last COPY fail?") → INFORMATION_SCHEMA table functions (QUERY_HISTORY(), COPY_HISTORY(), TASK_HISTORY()).

Also: ORGANIZATION_USAGE for multi-account orgs; READER_ACCOUNT_USAGE for reader accounts.
problems.lookfor: Latency vs retention trade-off and choosing per use case.
problems.followup: Build a daily snapshot of ACCOUNT_USAGE into your own tables — why? (Keep beyond 365 days, join with your own metadata, avoid repeated heavy scans.)

problems.title: Replication, failover and disaster recovery
problems.question: The business needs the analytics platform back within 1 hour if a cloud region fails, losing at most 15 minutes of data. Design it in Snowflake.
problems.answer:
Requirements: RTO 1 h, RPO 15 min.

  • Secondary account in another region (or cloud), same organisation.
  • Failover group containing databases and account objects — users, roles, grants, warehouses, resource monitors, integrations, network policies — so the secondary is usable without manual rebuild:
CREATE FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg
  OBJECT_TYPES = DATABASES, USERS, ROLES, WAREHOUSES, INTEGRATIONS, NETWORK POLICIES
  ALLOWED_DATABASES = raw, analytics
  ALLOWED_ACCOUNTS = myorg.prod_dr
  REPLICATION_SCHEDULE = '10 MINUTE';          -- inside the 15-min RPO
-- in the DR account:
CREATE FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg AS REPLICA OF myorg.prod_primary.prod_fg;
-- during an outage, in DR:
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg PRIMARY;
  • Client Redirect (connection object) so BI tools and apps use one URL that you repoint to the DR account — no reconfiguring clients.
  • Failover groups and client redirect require Business Critical edition (replication alone is available more broadly).

Beyond Snowflake — the parts people forget:

  • Pipelines: Airflow, dbt jobs, Snowpipe/stages and cloud storage notifications must also run in the DR region (or be repointable). Replicated pipes/stages need DR-side storage.
  • Data sources: if ingestion depends on the failed region, the DR side may have nothing new to load.
  • Runbook + quarterly DR drills; measure actual RTO/RPO.
  • Cost: replication transfer + compute + secondary storage — replicate only what the business needs within the RTO (raw history can often be rebuilt later).

Time Travel/Fail-safe is not DR — it protects against mistakes, not region loss.
problems.lookfor: RTO/RPO framing, failover groups with account objects, client redirect, edition, and non-Snowflake components.
problems.followup: How do you fail back after the primary recovers? (Replicate changes made in DR back to the original region, then promote again.)

problems.title: External tables vs Iceberg tables vs native tables
problems.question: Your company stores large datasets in S3 used by Spark, and wants Snowflake to query them. Compare external tables, Apache Iceberg tables and native tables. What would you recommend?
problems.answer:
Native table External table Iceberg table
data location Snowflake-managed storage your bucket (Parquet/CSV/JSON…) your bucket (Parquet + Iceberg metadata)
writes from Snowflake full DML read-only full DML when Snowflake is the catalog
performance best (micro-partition metadata) slower (limited metadata, file listing) close to native for most queries
open to other engines no (unless shared/exported) yes (files) yes — Spark, Trino, Flink… via the Iceberg catalog
features (Time Travel, clustering…) all few most

Iceberg catalog options:

  • Snowflake-managed (Snowflake is the catalog): Snowflake writes; other engines read through Snowflake's Iceberg REST catalog interface.
  • Externally managed: catalog is AWS Glue, Snowflake Open Catalog (managed Apache Polaris), or another REST catalog; Snowflake reads (and, with catalog-linked databases, can write) via a catalog integration. Storage is configured with an external volume.

Recommendation: for data shared with Spark, use Iceberg tables — one copy of data, open format, multiple engines. Decide which system is the writer/owner of each table (single-writer per table avoids conflicts). Keep native tables for Snowflake-only marts where you want every feature and maximum performance. External tables are now mostly a legacy option for querying raw files in place.

Watch-outs: small-file problems and compaction from other writers, catalog permissions across engines, cost of cloud storage requests, and egress if engines are in different regions.
problems.lookfor: Clear comparison, understanding catalogs and single-writer ownership, pragmatic recommendation.
problems.followup: How would you migrate a native table to Iceberg with minimal downtime? (CREATE ICEBERG TABLE … AS SELECT, dual-write or cut over during a quiet window, repoint views.)

problems.title: Snowpark, UDFs and stored procedures
problems.question: What is Snowpark? When would you use a Python UDF, a vectorized UDF, a UDTF, or a stored procedure? How does Snowpark differ from pulling data into pandas?
problems.answer:
Snowpark = DataFrame APIs (Python, Java, Scala) that build SQL lazily and push execution down into Snowflake warehouses. Data never leaves Snowflake; you get Python ergonomics with Snowflake scale and governance.

from snowflake.snowpark import Session
from snowflake.snowpark.functions import col, sum as sum_

df = (session.table("orders")
        .filter(col("status") == "SHIPPED")
        .group_by("customer_id")
        .agg(sum_("amount").alias("revenue")))
df.write.save_as_table("customer_revenue", mode="overwrite")   # runs as SQL in Snowflake

vs pandas: session.table("orders").to_pandas() pulls everything to the client — fine for small results, terrible for 500 M rows.

object use when
scalar UDF row-by-row logic not expressible in SQL (custom parsing, a Python library)
vectorized UDF same, but processes pandas batches — much faster for numeric/ML scoring
UDTF one input row → many output rows, or per-partition logic (e.g. sessionise per user with state)
stored procedure control flow: loops, DDL, calling multiple SQL statements, admin automation

Notes: third-party packages come from the Snowflake Anaconda channel (or an artifact repository / stage imports); memory-heavy work → Snowpark-optimized warehouses; prefer plain SQL when possible — the optimiser can't see inside UDFs.

Beyond that: Snowpark Container Services run containers (APIs, models, apps) next to the data.
problems.lookfor: Pushdown concept, choosing UDF types correctly, and "SQL first".
problems.followup: How do you unit-test Snowpark code? (Local testing framework / mock session for DataFrame logic; integration tests against a dev schema.)

problems.title: GDPR "right to be forgotten" in Snowflake
problems.question: A customer requests deletion of all their personal data. You run DELETE in every table. Is the data actually gone? Design a compliant approach.
problems.answer:
Not immediately. Deleted rows remain:

  • in Time Travel (up to the table's retention, up to 90 days),
  • then in Fail-safe (7 days for permanent tables),
  • in clones created earlier (they reference old micro-partitions),
  • in replicas, shares/consumer copies, unloaded files, BI extracts, and backups outside Snowflake.

Compliant design:

  1. Isolate PII. Keep personal attributes in a small set of PII tables keyed by a surrogate person_key; facts reference only the key. Deletion then touches few tables.
  2. Short retention on PII tables: DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1 (or 0) and transient where acceptable, so Time Travel doesn't keep data long. Document the total maximum persistence (retention + Fail-safe) in your privacy notice/DPA — regulators generally accept a defined, short backup window.
  3. Crypto-shredding / tokenisation: store PII encrypted or tokenised with a per-person key held outside; deleting the key makes all copies unreadable immediately, including history.
  4. Deletion pipeline: a request table → an automated job deletes/anonymises across all registered PII tables (driven by tags/classification), logs evidence, and propagates to downstream systems.
  5. Inventory: tags + ACCESS_HISTORY/lineage to find every place the data flows, including clones and replicas.
  6. Anonymise instead of delete where analytics must keep aggregates (remove the identifying link, keep the anonymous facts).
problems.lookfor: Knowing deleted ≠ gone, and a design answer (isolation, retention, crypto-shredding, automation, inventory).
problems.followup: How would you prove to an auditor that a deletion was completed? (Deletion log with request id, tables touched, row counts, timestamps; queries showing zero rows; retention configuration evidence.)

problems.title: Primary keys that aren't enforced
problems.question: A table has PRIMARY KEY (order_id), yet it contains duplicate order_ids. How is that possible? What's the point of declaring constraints in Snowflake then?
problems.answer:
Snowflake does not enforce PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE or FOREIGN KEY constraints on standard tables — only NOT NULL is enforced. (Hybrid tables are the exception: they enforce primary keys.) So duplicates are entirely possible.

Why declare them anyway:

  • Documentation and metadata for BI/ERD/catalog tools (they read constraints to infer joins).
  • Optimizer: with the RELY property, Snowflake can use constraints for join elimination — e.g. drop an unnecessary join to a dimension when no columns from it are selected.
ALTER TABLE dim_customer ADD CONSTRAINT pk_cust PRIMARY KEY (customer_id) RELY;

Only set RELY when you're sure the data satisfies it — otherwise query results can be wrong.

Enforcement must happen in the pipeline: dedup in loads, MERGE on keys, dbt unique + not_null + relationships tests (or contracts), and data-quality monitors (Snowflake data metric functions such as DUPLICATE_COUNT).
problems.lookfor: Knowing only NOT NULL is enforced, RELY/join elimination, and where enforcement really happens.
problems.followup: Write a query to find duplicate keys and how many extra rows they create (GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, sum of COUNT(*) - 1).

problems.title: Loading messy files: schema detection and options
problems.question: A new source sends Parquet files whose columns sometimes get added or reordered, plus CSVs with headers, quotes and occasional bad dates. Which COPY/file-format features do you use?
problems.answer:
Parquet with changing columns:

-- create the table from the files' schema
CREATE TABLE raw.events USING TEMPLATE (
  SELECT ARRAY_AGG(OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*))
  FROM TABLE(INFER_SCHEMA(LOCATION => '@stg/events/', FILE_FORMAT => 'parquet_fmt')));

ALTER TABLE raw.events SET ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION = TRUE;  -- new columns added automatically

COPY INTO raw.events FROM @stg/events/
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = parquet_fmt)
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE         -- order no longer matters
INCLUDE_METADATA = (source_file = METADATA$FILENAME,
                    file_row = METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER);

CSV with quirks:

CREATE FILE FORMAT csv_fmt TYPE = CSV
  PARSE_HEADER = TRUE                     -- enables MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME for CSV
  FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"'
  NULL_IF = ('', 'NULL', 'N/A')
  EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL = TRUE
  DATE_FORMAT = 'AUTO'
  ERROR_ON_COLUMN_COUNT_MISMATCH = FALSE
  ENCODING = 'UTF8';

Robust pattern for bad values: land raw columns as VARCHAR, then convert in staging with TRY_TO_DATE, TRY_TO_NUMBER and route failures to a quarantine table — loads never fail, and bad data is visible.

Also: ON_ERROR choice, PURGE = TRUE to delete loaded files (or lifecycle rules on the bucket), PATTERN = '.*orders_.*[.]csv', and file sizing (~100–250 MB compressed).
problems.lookfor: Schema detection/evolution, metadata columns for lineage, and the land-as-string-then-TRY_ pattern.
problems.followup: How do you load only files modified in the last day from a huge bucket? (Partitioned paths /date=YYYY-MM-DD/, PATTERN, or event-driven Snowpipe instead of listing.)

problems.title: AI inside Snowflake: Cortex functions, Cortex Search, Cortex Analyst
problems.question: Leadership asks: "How can we use AI on our Snowflake data without sending it outside?" Explain the main Snowflake AI building blocks and a sensible first use case.
problems.answer:
• AI SQL functions — LLM operations as SQL functions, running inside Snowflake's security boundary: e.g. AI_COMPLETE (prompt an LLM), AI_CLASSIFY, AI_FILTER (natural-language WHERE condition), AI_AGG (summarise across rows), AI_SENTIMENT, translation and extraction functions. (Older equivalents live under SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.*, e.g. COMPLETE.)
SELECT ticket_id,
       AI_CLASSIFY(body, ['billing', 'bug', 'feature request', 'other']) AS category,
       AI_SENTIMENT(body) AS sentiment
FROM support_tickets
WHERE created_at >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE);
  • Cortex Search — managed hybrid (vector + keyword) search over text, for RAG chatbots on documents, tickets and wikis.
  • Cortex Analyst — natural-language questions → SQL, grounded in semantic views (business definitions of tables, relationships, metrics). Accuracy depends heavily on a good semantic layer.
  • Agents that combine Analyst (structured) and Search (unstructured) to answer questions; Snowflake's coding agent (CoCo) helps build pipelines.

Sensible first use case: classify and summarise support tickets or call notes with AI functions in a dbt model — easy to measure, no new infrastructure, and immediately useful.

Architect concerns: cost (token-based credits — test on samples, filter rows first, cache results in tables instead of calling on every query), governance (masking and RBAC still apply), quality (evaluate outputs on a labelled sample), and semantic layer ownership (who maintains metric definitions).
problems.lookfor: Concrete building blocks, a pragmatic first use case, and cost/quality/governance thinking rather than hype.
problems.followup: How do you avoid re-running an LLM function on the same rows every day? (Incremental model: only new rows get classified; store results.)

problems.title: Editions: which features need what
problems.question: Your client is on Standard edition and wants 30-day Time Travel, multi-cluster warehouses, masking policies, private connectivity and failover. What do they need?
problems.answer:
feature minimum edition
Time Travel beyond 1 day (up to 90) Enterprise
Multi-cluster warehouses Enterprise
Column masking, row access policies, tag-based masking Enterprise
Materialized views, search optimization, query acceleration Enterprise
Access history Enterprise
Private connectivity (PrivateLink etc.), Tri-Secret Secure, HIPAA/PCI-ready setups Business Critical
Failover/failback groups and Client Redirect Business Critical
Dedicated, isolated environment Virtual Private Snowflake (VPS)

So this client needs Business Critical. Credit prices rise with edition, so architects often justify the upgrade with specific requirements (compliance, DR) — or keep non-critical workloads in a separate lower-edition account.
problems.lookfor: Knowing the big boundaries (Enterprise vs Business Critical) and framing cost vs requirement.
problems.followup: Can different accounts in one organisation have different editions? (Yes — a common pattern to keep costs down.)

problems.title: Materializations — which one, when?
problems.question: Explain dbt's materializations and when you'd choose each. What's a sensible default per layer?
problems.answer:
materialization what dbt builds use when
view a view light transformations, staging models, always-fresh data, low storage
table full rebuild each run (CTAS) marts queried often; data small enough to rebuild quickly
incremental inserts/merges only new or changed rows large or growing tables where full rebuilds are slow/costly
ephemeral no object — inlined as a CTE into downstream models tiny reusable logic (use sparingly)
materialized_view / dynamic_table (Snowflake) warehouse-managed refresh near-real-time freshness managed by the warehouse
snapshot (separate resource) SCD Type 2 history table tracking changes to mutable sources

Sensible defaults:

  • staging: views (1:1 with sources, renaming/casting).
  • intermediate: views or ephemeral; tables if reused heavily or complex.
  • marts: tables; incremental when large.

Decision drivers: query frequency vs build cost, data volume, freshness needs, and how many models depend on it. Many views stacked on views can make the final query very slow — materialise at sensible checkpoints.
problems.lookfor: Practical trade-offs and layer conventions, not just definitions.
problems.followup: A view-based staging layer makes the marts build slowly. Options? (Materialise heavy staging models as tables, or incremental; check query profile of mart builds.)

problems.title: Incremental models done right
problems.question: Write an incremental model for a large events table. How do you handle late-arriving events, and what does is_incremental() actually check?
problems.answer:
{{ config(
    materialized = 'incremental',
    unique_key   = 'event_id',
    incremental_strategy = 'merge',
    on_schema_change = 'append_new_columns'
) }}

SELECT event_id, user_id, event_type, event_ts, _loaded_at
FROM {{ source('app', 'events') }}

{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- 3-day lookback catches late-arriving rows; unique_key prevents duplicates
  WHERE _loaded_at > (SELECT DATEADD(day, -3, MAX(_loaded_at)) FROM {{ this }})
{% endif %}
  • is_incremental() is TRUE only when all hold: the model is materialized incremental, the target table already exists, and you're not running with --full-refresh.
  • {{ this }} refers to the existing target table.
  • Filter on load time (_loaded_at), not event time, when possible — event time can arrive late; load time only increases. If you must use event time, add a lookback window.
  • The lookback re-processes some rows; unique_key + merge makes that safe (idempotent).
  • Avoid SELECT MAX(...) on a huge target every run if it's slow — Snowflake answers MAX from metadata quickly on many tables, but a clustered date column helps.
  • Keep a way to rebuild: dbt build -s model --full-refresh (and protect giant models with full_refresh: false config so nobody rebuilds them by accident).
problems.lookfor: Correct is_incremental semantics, load-time vs event-time filtering, lookback + unique_key idempotency.
problems.followup: How do you backfill one month of a huge incremental model without a full refresh? (Microbatch with --event-time-start/--event-time-end, or a var-driven date filter.)

problems.title: Incremental strategies on Snowflake: merge, delete+insert, append, insert_overwrite, microbatch
problems.question: Compare dbt's incremental strategies on Snowflake. Which would you choose for (a) an append-only log, (b) a table where rows are updated by key, (c) daily partitions that are fully recomputed, (d) a 5-year fact table that needs easy backfills?
problems.answer:
strategy SQL dbt generates good for watch out
append INSERT append-only data with no duplicates re-runs create duplicates
merge (Snowflake default) MERGE on unique_key updates by key source must be unique per key; scans target to match — slow on huge tables without predicates
delete+insert DELETE matching keys, then INSERT replacing groups of rows (e.g. a whole day) key need not be unique in the new data
insert_overwrite on Snowflake overwrites the whole table (no partitions) rarely what you want here very different meaning than on BigQuery/Spark
microbatch splits work into time batches (on Snowflake runs delete+insert per batch) large time-series facts, backfills, retrying failed batches needs event_time, batch_size, begin configs

Answers:

  • (a) append — or merge if duplicates can arrive.
  • (b) merge with a deduplicated source; add incremental_predicates to limit the target scan: e.g. only match target rows from the last 7 days.
  • (c) delete+insert with unique_key='event_date' — replaces whole days atomically.
  • (d) microbatch:
{{ config(materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='microbatch',
          event_time='event_ts', batch_size='day', begin='2021-01-01', lookback=2) }}
SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_events') }}   -- dbt auto-filters upstream refs by event_time

Backfill: dbt run -s fct_events --event-time-start 2026-01-01 --event-time-end 2026-02-01. Failed batches can be retried individually with dbt retry.

Performance tip for big merges:

{{ config(incremental_strategy='merge', unique_key='order_id',
          incremental_predicates=["DBT_INTERNAL_DEST.order_date >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE)"]) }}

— only safe if updates never touch older rows.
problems.lookfor: Precise semantics per strategy, knowing Snowflake's insert_overwrite caveat, microbatch, incremental predicates.
problems.followup: Why can merge be slower than delete+insert on Snowflake for large daily loads? (MERGE has to join against the target to find matches; delete+insert by date prunes by partition and inserts cheaply.)

problems.title: Adding a column to an incremental model
problems.question: You add a new column discount_pct to an existing incremental model. What happens on the next run? What are the on_schema_change options, and how do you get historical values filled?
problems.answer:
Default on_schema_change = 'ignore': the new column is silently not added to the target table — the model runs, and the column never appears. Options:

setting behaviour
ignore (default) target schema unchanged; new columns dropped
fail run fails when schemas differ — forces a conscious decision
append_new_columns adds new columns; never removes
sync_all_columns adds new and removes missing columns; handles type changes

None of them backfills historical rows — old rows get NULL in the new column. To populate history: run --full-refresh (if affordable), or a targeted backfill (a one-off UPDATE/merge for older data, or microbatch backfill over the date range).

Production view: use fail or append_new_columns for critical models, be careful with sync_all_columns (dropping columns breaks consumers), and pair schema changes with model contracts so changes are deliberate and reviewed.
problems.lookfor: Knowing the silent default, the four options, and that none backfill.
problems.followup: Changing a column's type (e.g. INT → VARCHAR) in an incremental model — what happens? (Depends on adapter; sync_all_columns can alter; otherwise rebuild or migrate.)

problems.title: Snapshots: timestamp vs check, hard deletes, and current rows
problems.question: How do dbt snapshots work? When do you use the timestamp vs check strategy? How are deleted source rows handled? What do dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to mean?
problems.answer:
A snapshot implements SCD Type 2: each run compares the source to the snapshot table and, for changed rows, closes the old version and inserts a new one.

# snapshots/customers.yml  (YAML snapshot config, dbt 1.9+)
snapshots:
  - name: customers_snapshot
    relation: source('crm', 'customers')
    config:
      schema: snapshots
      unique_key: customer_id
      strategy: timestamp
      updated_at: updated_at
      hard_deletes: invalidate        # ignore (default) | invalidate | new_record
      dbt_valid_to_current: "to_date('9999-12-31')"   # instead of NULL for current rows
  • timestamp strategy: a row changed if updated_at is newer. Efficient and reliable — use it when the source has a trustworthy updated_at.
  • check strategy: compares the listed check_cols (or all). Use when there's no reliable timestamp. More expensive, and it misses changes that revert within one interval.
  • dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to: the period each version was current; current rows have dbt_valid_to NULL (or the configured far-future date). Also dbt_scd_id, dbt_updated_at.
  • Hard deletes: default ignore (deleted rows stay "current" forever); invalidate closes them; new_record inserts a deletion row (with dbt_is_deleted).

Practical points:

  • A snapshot only captures what it sees when it runs — changes between runs are collapsed. Run snapshots frequently enough, or snapshot from a CDC log instead.
  • Snapshots hold irreplaceable history: keep them non-transient, protect them from full refresh, back them up.
  • Snapshot sources as raw as possible (selecting from sources, not heavily transformed models).
problems.lookfor: Strategy trade-offs, hard deletes, irreplaceability of snapshot data.
problems.followup: Point-in-time join: what was the customer's tier at order time? (Join on customer_id and order_ts >= dbt_valid_from AND order_ts < COALESCE(dbt_valid_to, '9999-12-31').)

problems.title: Testing strategy in dbt
problems.question: Describe the types of tests in dbt and a sensible testing strategy for a large project. How do you stop noisy tests from blocking production?
problems.answer:
Types:

  • Generic data tests in YAML: unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships — plus package tests (dbt_utils, dbt-expectations) and your own custom generic tests (a Jinja macro with {% test %}).
  • Singular data tests: a .sql file in tests/ that returns failing rows.
  • Unit tests (dbt 1.8+): test model logic with mocked inputs (see unit tests problem).
  • Source freshness: loaded_at_field + warn_after / error_after.
  • Model contracts: enforce column names/types at build time.
models:
  - name: fct_orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: status
        data_tests:
          - accepted_values:
              arguments:
                values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'returned']
              config: {severity: warn}
      - name: customer_id
        data_tests:
          - relationships:
              arguments: {to: ref('dim_customers'), field: customer_id}
              config:
                where: "order_date >= dateadd(day, -30, current_date)"
                error_if: ">100"
                warn_if: ">0"
                store_failures: true

(Older projects write tests: and put arguments directly under the test — both styles appear in interviews.)

Strategy:

  • Every model: primary key unique + not_null (catches fan-out and duplicates — the #1 bug).
  • Sources: freshness + key tests at the entry point — catch problems before they spread.
  • Marts: business rules (accepted values, relationships, reconciliation totals against source).
  • Use severity, warn_if, error_if to separate "page someone" from "look at it tomorrow".
  • where configs to test only recent data on huge tables.
  • store_failures to save failing rows for debugging.
  • dbt build runs tests right after each model, so downstream models don't build on bad data.
problems.lookfor: Breadth of test types, a prioritised strategy, severity thresholds, and dbt build ordering.
problems.followup: Tests run fine but data is still "wrong" for the business. What's missing? (Reconciliation tests vs source systems, anomaly detection on volumes/metrics, contracts with producers.)

problems.title: Unit tests: testing logic, not data
problems.question: What are dbt unit tests and how are they different from data tests? Write one for a model that flags orders over ₹10,000 as is_large.
problems.answer:
Data tests check the data after it's built (is it unique, not null…). Unit tests (dbt 1.8+) check the model's SQL logic with small, hand-written inputs and expected outputs — before touching real data. They catch logic bugs (wrong boundary, wrong join) regardless of what production data happens to contain.

unit_tests:
  - name: test_is_large_order_boundary
    model: fct_orders
    given:
      - input: ref('stg_orders')
        rows:
          - {order_id: 1, amount: 9999}
          - {order_id: 2, amount: 10000}
          - {order_id: 3, amount: 10001}
          - {order_id: 4, amount: null}
    expect:
      rows:
        - {order_id: 1, is_large: false}
        - {order_id: 2, is_large: false}   # "over" 10,000 → strictly greater
        - {order_id: 3, is_large: true}
        - {order_id: 4, is_large: false}
  • Only the columns you list matter; inputs can be given as dict rows, CSV or SQL.
  • For incremental models, you can test the incremental path with overrides: macros: is_incremental: true and provide this as an input.
  • Run them in CI/dev, not on every production run (they don't depend on prod data): dbt test --select test_type:unit.
  • Best for complex logic: regex parsing, date edge cases (month ends, time zones), CASE ladders, window logic.
problems.lookfor: Clear distinction, boundary/NULL cases in the example, and where unit tests run.
problems.followup: How do you unit test a model that uses current_date? (Override the macro/var that provides the date, or pass the date as a var.)

problems.title: Contracts, versions, access — governing models at scale
problems.question: Your marts are consumed by BI, ML and other teams' dbt projects. A column rename last month broke three dashboards. How do model contracts, versions, access and groups prevent this?
problems.answer:
• Model contract — a promise about the shape of the output. With contract: {enforced: true}, dbt checks column names and data types at build time (and applies supported constraints such as not_null); the build fails if the SQL doesn't match.
models:
  - name: dim_customers
    config:
      contract: {enforced: true}
      access: public
      group: customer_domain
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        data_type: number
        constraints: [{type: not_null}]
      - name: full_name
        data_type: varchar
  • Model versions — make breaking changes safely: publish v2 alongside v1, give consumers a deprecation date, then remove v1.
    latest_version: 2
    versions:
      - v: 1
        deprecation_date: 2027-01-31
      - v: 2
        columns:
          - include: all
            exclude: [full_name]
          - name: first_name
            data_type: varchar

Consumers pin with ref('dim_customers', v=1).

  • Access — private (only within its group), protected (within the project; default), public (other projects can ref it).
  • Groups — ownership: which team owns a set of models, with contact info.
  • dbt Mesh — multiple projects referencing each other's public models (cross-project ref), each team owning its domain (available on the dbt platform's enterprise plans).

Architect view: treat public models as APIs: contract + version + owner + deprecation policy + changelog; CI checks that detect breaking changes (dbt flags contract changes on modified public models); exposures to know which dashboards depend on what.
problems.lookfor: Data-products thinking: contracts as APIs, versioned change management, ownership.
problems.followup: How would you find every dashboard affected by a column change? (Exposures in dbt, BI-tool lineage, or warehouse access history.)

problems.title: Slim CI: build only what changed
problems.question: Your dbt project has 1,500 models; CI builds everything and takes 90 minutes. Design a fast CI process.
problems.answer:
Slim CI = build and test only modified models and their downstream dependents, reading unchanged parents from production.

# 1. Get production's manifest (artifact from the last prod run)
#    e.g. download to ./prod-artifacts/manifest.json

# 2. Build only changed models + children, in a PR-specific schema
dbt build \
  --select state:modified+ \
  --defer --state ./prod-artifacts \
  --target ci                        # schema like ci_pr_1234
  • state:modified compares the current project to the prod manifest (SQL, configs, macros it uses…). The + adds downstream models.
  • --defer means: when a selected model refers to an unbuilt parent, use the production relation instead of failing.
  • Alternatively dbt clone --select state:modified+ --state … creates zero-copy clones of prod tables into the CI schema first — on Snowflake that's instant and lets incremental models run their incremental path in CI.
  • Include state:modified.body, .configs, .contract selectors as needed; --empty (dbt 1.8+) for a quick schema-only dry run with no data.
  • Clean up the CI schema when the PR closes.

Also in CI: SQL linting (SQLFluff), dbt parse/compile errors, unit tests, contract/breaking-change checks, and data diffing on key models (compare row counts/values between PR build and prod, e.g. audit_helper).

Result: typical PRs touch a few models → CI runs in minutes, with lower warehouse cost.
problems.lookfor: state:modified+, --defer, prod manifest handling, clones, and extra CI checks.
problems.followup: What does state:modified miss? (Changes in upstream data rather than code; env-var-driven logic; some macro changes in older versions — hence also run a scheduled full build/test.)

problems.title: Node selection syntax
problems.question: Write commands to: (1) run fct_orders and everything upstream; (2) everything downstream of stg_customers; (3) a model, its parents, and all parents of its children; (4) all models tagged finance except those in the legacy folder; (5) only the parents two levels up.
problems.answer:
dbt run --select +fct_orders                        # 1  upstream + model
dbt run --select stg_customers+                     # 2  model + downstream
dbt build --select @dim_customers                   # 3  "at" operator: model, descendants, and
                                                    #    all ancestors of those descendants
dbt run --select tag:finance --exclude path:models/legacy   # 4
dbt run --select 2+fct_orders                       # 5  up to 2 generations of parents

More selectors: path:models/marts, config.materialized:incremental, source:crm+, resource_type:snapshot, test_type:unit, state:modified+, result:error+ (with --state from a previous run). Intersection uses commas: --select tag:finance,config.materialized:table. Union uses spaces.

Reusable named selections go in selectors.yml (e.g. a nightly_finance selector) so jobs don't copy long CLI strings.

@ is the one people forget: it's what you need when building a model in a fresh environment so its children's other parents exist too.
problems.lookfor: Fluency, the @ operator, union vs intersection, selectors.yml.
problems.followup: Re-run only models that failed (or were skipped) in the last run? (dbt retry.)

problems.title: ref, source and why hard-coded table names hurt
problems.question: Why use {{ ref() }} and {{ source() }} instead of writing analytics.marts.orders? What are sources for besides naming?
problems.answer:
ref():

  • Builds the DAG — dbt knows dependencies and runs models in the right order.
  • Resolves to the right environment: dev schema in dev, prod in prod, CI schema in CI — the same code works everywhere.
  • Enables lineage graphs, docs, --defer, selection with +, and impact analysis.

source():

  • Declares raw tables once in YAML (database/schema/identifier can vary by environment).
  • Freshness checks: loaded_at_field with warn_after/error_after → dbt source freshness.
  • Tests on raw data at the entry point.
  • Lineage starts at sources; source:crm+ selects everything built from a system.

Hard-coding breaks environment isolation (dev queries hitting prod), hides dependencies (wrong build order, models silently stale), and makes renames painful.

Rule: models reference other models only with ref, raw data only with source, and staging models are the only layer that reads sources directly.
problems.lookfor: DAG + environment resolution + freshness, and the staging-only-reads-sources rule.
problems.followup: How do you reference a table owned by another team's dbt project? (Cross-project ref with dbt Mesh, or declare it as a source.)

problems.title: The custom schema surprise: generate_schema_name
problems.question: You set +schema: marts on your marts folder. In production the tables land in analytics_marts instead of marts. Why? How do you make prod use marts exactly while dev stays isolated?
problems.answer:
dbt's default generate_schema_name macro concatenates target schema + custom schema: <target.schema>_<custom_schema>. With target.schema = analytics, +schema: marts → analytics_marts. This is by design: in dev (target.schema = dbt_alice) you get dbt_alice_marts, so developers never overwrite each other or prod.

Override the macro to behave differently per environment:

-- macros/generate_schema_name.sql
{% macro generate_schema_name(custom_schema_name, node) -%}
    {%- if target.name == 'prod' and custom_schema_name is not none -%}
        {{ custom_schema_name | trim }}                 {# prod: exactly "marts" #}
    {%- elif custom_schema_name is none -%}
        {{ target.schema }}
    {%- else -%}
        {{ target.schema }}_{{ custom_schema_name | trim }}   {# dev/CI: dbt_alice_marts #}
    {%- endif -%}
{%- endmacro %}

dbt also ships generate_schema_name_for_env which implements this pattern. The same idea applies to generate_database_name and generate_alias_name.
problems.lookfor: Knowing the concatenation default, why it exists, and the override.
problems.followup: Two models in different folders want the same table name in different schemas — how? (alias config.)

problems.title: Hooks, grants and query tags
problems.question: After each model builds you must grant SELECT to the BI role, tag queries for cost tracking, and once per run log the run to an audit table. How do you do each in dbt?
problems.answer:
# dbt_project.yml
models:
  my_project:
    +query_tag: "dbt_{{ target.name }}"          # Snowflake query tag on every query
    marts:
      +grants:
        select: ['BI_READER']                    # declarative grants (dbt 1.2+)
      +post-hook:
        - "ALTER TABLE {{ this }} SET COMMENT = 'Built by dbt run {{ invocation_id }}'"

on-run-start:
  - "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS audit.dbt_runs (invocation_id STRING, started_at TIMESTAMP, target STRING)"
on-run-end:
  - "INSERT INTO audit.dbt_runs VALUES ('{{ invocation_id }}', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), '{{ target.name }}')"
  - "{{ log_results(results) }}"                 # a macro that writes each model's status/timing
  • grants config is better than post-hook GRANT statements: dbt applies only the needed changes and re-applies them after table rebuilds. On Snowflake also consider copy_grants: true, or rely on future grants.
  • pre/post-hooks run before/after each model — for things like ALTER SESSION, clustering, comments, row access policies.
  • on-run-start / on-run-end run once per invocation; on-run-end receives results (status, timing, rows affected) — great for run logging/observability.
  • query_tag (Snowflake) for cost attribution per model/project/env.
  • Hooks are SQL strings rendered with Jinja; keep them idempotent.
problems.lookfor: Using grants instead of hooks for permissions, on-run-end results for observability, cost tagging.
problems.followup: Run each heavy model on a bigger warehouse? (snowflake_warehouse config per model/folder.)

problems.title: Ephemeral models — useful or harmful?
problems.question: A teammate made 40 intermediate models ephemeral "to save storage". Builds got slower and debugging got harder. Explain why and when ephemeral is appropriate.
problems.answer:
Ephemeral models aren't built in the warehouse; dbt inlines their SQL as CTEs into every downstream model.

Problems at scale:

  • Repeated computation: an ephemeral model used by 5 downstream models is computed 5 times.
  • Giant compiled SQL: chains of ephemeral models produce very long queries that are hard to read and optimise.
  • Hard to debug: you can't SELECT * FROM an ephemeral model to inspect its output.
  • Can't be queried by other tools; limited support in some operations (e.g. can't be the target of some macros, tricky with dbt show).

Appropriate: very small, light logic (a few columns renamed/derived) used by one or two models, early in the DAG.

Better alternatives: views (cheap — no storage, inspectable, one definition) or tables for heavy, reused intermediate steps. Storage on Snowflake is cheap relative to compute; computing the same thing many times costs more.
problems.lookfor: Understanding inlining, compute vs storage trade-off, debuggability.
problems.followup: How do you find models that are expensive and heavily reused? (Model timing from run_results.json + number of children in the manifest.)

problems.title: Project structure: staging, intermediate, marts
problems.question: Describe how you structure a dbt project and the naming conventions. What belongs in each layer?
problems.answer:
models/
  staging/            one folder per source system
    stripe/
      _stripe__sources.yml
      _stripe__models.yml
      stg_stripe__payments.sql
  intermediate/       business logic building blocks, by domain
    finance/
      int_payments_pivoted_to_orders.sql
  marts/              business-facing, by domain/consumer
    finance/
      fct_orders.sql
      dim_customers.sql
  • Staging (stg_<source>__<entity>): 1:1 with source tables; rename, cast, light cleanup (e.g. cents → currency), dedupe. No joins, no business logic. Usually views. The only layer that uses source().
  • Intermediate (int_…): joins, aggregations, re-graining — reusable steps toward marts. Not exposed to end users.
  • Marts (fct_, dim_, or wide entity tables): the products for BI/ML — documented, tested, contracted.

Conventions that matter: consistent names, a primary key on every model, YAML docs per folder, a _<dir>__models.yml pattern, macros in macros/, seeds only for small static lookup data, and tests concentrated at sources and marts.
problems.lookfor: Clear layer responsibilities and consistency.
problems.followup: Where would you put a model used by both finance and marketing marts? (Intermediate or a shared mart; avoid marts depending on other domains' marts when possible.)

problems.title: dbt on Snowflake: transient, clustering, warehouses, copy_grants
problems.question: List the Snowflake-specific dbt configs you'd consider for a 3 TB incremental fact table and its marts.
problems.answer:
{{ config(
    materialized = 'incremental',
    unique_key   = 'order_line_id',
    incremental_strategy = 'merge',
    transient    = false,              -- dbt-snowflake default is TRANSIENT (no Fail-safe)
    cluster_by   = ['order_date'],     -- adds a clustering key
    snowflake_warehouse = 'TRANSFORM_L_WH',   -- bigger warehouse just for this model
    copy_grants  = true,               -- keep grants when the table is recreated
    query_tag    = 'dbt_fct_order_lines'
) }}
  • transient: default true in dbt-snowflake → no Fail-safe and ≤1 day Time Travel. Set false for anything hard to rebuild (incremental history, snapshots).
  • cluster_by / automatic_clustering: for large tables with consistent filters; dbt orders data by the key on full builds.
  • snowflake_warehouse: right-size per model instead of one big warehouse for everything.
  • copy_grants: preserve grants on CREATE OR REPLACE.
  • secure: create secure views (for sharing).
  • query_tag: cost attribution.
  • Dynamic tables: materialized='dynamic_table' with target_lag and snowflake_warehouse.
  • Python models run via Snowpark on Snowflake.
problems.lookfor: Knowing the transient default and practical per-model tuning.
problems.followup: Why might cluster_by on a small table be harmful? (Reclustering cost with no pruning benefit.)

problems.title: A dbt run that takes 4 hours
problems.question: The nightly dbt build takes 4 hours and keeps growing. How do you analyse and speed it up?
problems.answer:
1. Measure, don't guess.

  • run_results.json → execution time per model; the critical path in the DAG (dbt docs / artifacts tools / orchestrator Gantt view).
  • Snowflake query history by query_tag → which models consume the most credits, spill, or scan the most.

2. Fix the biggest offenders:

  • Convert large full-rebuild tables to incremental (or microbatch).
  • Add incremental_predicates to big merges; switch to delete+insert by date where appropriate.
  • Stop rebuilding unchanged history (full refresh weekly at most, not nightly).
  • Rewrite slow SQL: filter early, avoid fan-out joins, avoid views-on-views chains for heavy logic.

3. Parallelism:

  • Increase threads (Snowflake handles many concurrent queries; pair with a multi-cluster warehouse if queuing appears).
  • Break long serial chains in the DAG; a single slow model on the critical path dominates total time.

4. Right-size compute: larger warehouse for the few heavy models (snowflake_warehouse config), small for the rest.

5. Run less:

  • Not everything needs to run nightly: tag models by schedule (hourly/daily/weekly).
  • Source freshness-driven runs: --select source_status:fresher+ builds only models whose sources got new data.
  • Make tests cheaper: where configs on huge tables, fewer redundant tests.

6. Platform: newer dbt engines (dbt v2 / Fusion) parse and compile faster on huge projects, but SQL execution time is usually the real bottleneck.
problems.lookfor: Data-driven approach, critical path thinking, incremental/parallelism/compute levers, and "run less".
problems.followup: How would you set and monitor an SLA "marts ready by 6 am"? (Orchestrator SLA alert, model timing trends, freshness checks on marts.)

problems.title: Debugging a failing dbt model
problems.question: A model fails in production with a SQL error you can't reproduce locally. How do you debug?
problems.answer:
1. Read the compiled SQL: target/compiled/<project>/models/...sql (Jinja rendered) and target/run/... (the actual DDL/DML executed, e.g. the MERGE). Paste into Snowflake and run it.
  2. Compare environments: the difference is usually target (prod vars, target.name branches in macros), different data (NULLs, new values, duplicates), different permissions, or an incremental run in prod vs full build locally.
  3. Reproduce the incremental path locally: build once, then run again (or use --defer to prod).
  4. dbt debug (connection/profile), dbt compile -s model, dbt show -s model --limit 10 (preview results), dbt ls -s +model (what would run).
  5. Logs: logs/dbt.log, --debug flag; Snowflake query history with the dbt query_tag to see the exact failing statement and error.
  6. --empty builds models with zero rows to validate SQL and schemas cheaply.
  7. After fixing: dbt retry to resume from the failure point.

Typical root causes: schema drift in a source, duplicate keys in a merge source (non-deterministic merge error), data type overflow, a reserved word as a column, permissions after an object was recreated.
problems.lookfor: Going to compiled/run SQL first, environment differences, the incremental-path trap.
problems.followup: How do you stop the same class of bug next time? (Add a test, contract, or source freshness/schema check that would have caught it.)

problems.title: Packages worth knowing
problems.question: Which dbt packages do you use regularly and for what? How would you validate a migration from a legacy SQL pipeline to dbt?
problems.answer:
• dbt_utils: generate_surrogate_key, date_spine, star (select all columns except…), union_relations, pivot, deduplicate, tests like equal_rowcount, expression_is_true, unique_combination_of_columns, accepted_range.
  • dbt-expectations: Great-Expectations-style tests (value ranges, regex, row counts between, recency).
  • audit_helper: compare two relations or queries row-by-row — the migration tool: compare_relations, compare_queries, compare_column_values.
  • codegen: generate source YAML and base models from existing tables.
  • dbt_project_evaluator: checks the project against best-practice rules (naming, direct source references in marts, missing tests/docs).
  • Observability packages (e.g. ones that upload run artifacts into tables).

Migration validation with audit_helper:

{% set old_query %} SELECT * FROM legacy.reporting.orders_summary {% endset %}
{% set new_query %} SELECT * FROM {{ ref('fct_orders_summary') }} {% endset %}
{{ audit_helper.compare_queries(a_query=old_query, b_query=new_query,
                                primary_key='order_id', summarize=true) }}

Output: % of rows in both, only in A, only in B. Then drill into mismatching columns. Run it for several periods, and reconcile totals (revenue, counts) with business owners before switching consumers.

Pin package versions in packages.yml and upgrade deliberately.
problems.lookfor: Concrete usage, especially the migration-validation workflow.
problems.followup: What's a surrogate key and why hash it? (generate_surrogate_key → deterministic MD5 of natural key columns; stable across rebuilds, handles composite keys.)

problems.title: Orchestrating dbt with Airflow
problems.question: How would you run dbt from Airflow? Compare running dbt build as one task, rendering each model as a task (Cosmos), and triggering dbt platform jobs.
problems.answer:
approach pros cons
One task: dbt build (BashOperator/KubernetesPodOperator) simple; dbt handles ordering and parallelism a failure means re-running from Airflow is coarse (use dbt retry); no per-model visibility in Airflow
Cosmos (astronomer-cosmos): each model/test becomes an Airflow task or task group model-level retries, visibility, mix dbt with non-dbt tasks precisely huge DAGs for big projects; parsing overhead; Airflow scheduling overhead per model
Trigger a dbt platform (Cloud) job via the provider operator dbt platform handles environments, docs, CI; Airflow just coordinates two systems to monitor; licence cost

Good practice regardless of approach:

  • Run dbt in an isolated environment (container/venv) so dbt dependencies don't conflict with Airflow's.
  • Pass the logical date as a var for date-partitioned models — not "today".
  • Trigger dbt when data lands (Airflow assets/sensors) instead of a fixed time.
  • Split by domain/schedule (--select tag:hourly), not one monolithic run.
  • Persist run_results.json/manifest.json for observability and slim runs.

For most teams: start with one task per domain selection, move to Cosmos when model-level control in Airflow is really needed.
problems.lookfor: Trade-offs, isolation, logical dates, event-driven triggering.
problems.followup: Airflow retries a failed dbt task — how do you avoid re-running 400 successful models? (dbt retry using the previous run's artifacts, or Cosmos task-level retries.)

problems.title: Semantic layer and metrics
problems.question: Why do companies add a semantic layer (dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow) on top of marts? How does it relate to AI analytics?
problems.answer:
Problem: "revenue" is calculated differently in five dashboards (gross vs net, with/without refunds, by order date vs ship date). Metrics live in BI tools, spreadsheets and ad-hoc SQL.

A semantic layer defines entities, dimensions, measures and metrics once, in code, and generates the SQL for any requested slice:

semantic_models:
  - name: orders
    model: ref('fct_orders')
    defaults: {agg_time_dimension: order_date}
    entities:
      - {name: order_id, type: primary}
      - {name: customer, type: foreign, expr: customer_id}
    dimensions:
      - {name: order_date, type: time, type_params: {time_granularity: day}}
      - {name: channel, type: categorical}
    measures:
      - {name: net_revenue, agg: sum, expr: amount - refunds}

metrics:
  - name: net_revenue
    label: Net revenue
    type: simple
    type_params: {measure: net_revenue}

Benefits: consistent numbers everywhere, metrics reviewed in git, joins handled automatically (MetricFlow knows the entity graph), and BI tools/notebooks/APIs query metrics by name.

AI link: text-to-SQL over raw tables guesses joins and definitions. Grounding AI on a semantic layer (dbt Semantic Layer, or Snowflake semantic views for Cortex Analyst) gives much more accurate, governed answers — the AI chooses metrics and dimensions, and the layer writes correct SQL.
problems.lookfor: The business problem, the core concepts, and the AI-grounding argument.
problems.followup: Semantic layer in dbt vs in the BI tool vs in Snowflake semantic views — how to choose? (Where most consumers are; avoid defining metrics twice; check integrations with your BI and AI tools.)

problems.title: Airflow architecture — components and what each does
problems.question: Name Airflow's main components and what each does. What changed in Airflow 3's architecture?
problems.answer:
• Scheduler — decides which task instances should run (schedules, dependencies, retries) and hands them to the executor.
  • DAG processor — parses DAG files into serialized DAGs stored in the metadata DB. In Airflow 3 it's a separate process you must run (airflow dag-processor).
  • Executor — how tasks run: locally, on Celery workers, as Kubernetes pods, etc.
  • Workers — execute task code.
  • Triggerer — runs async triggers for deferrable operators/sensors (waiting without occupying a worker slot).
  • Metadata database (Postgres/MySQL) — state of DAG runs, task instances, connections, variables, XComs.
  • API server / UI — in Airflow 3 the web server is replaced by an API server that serves the UI and the REST API.

Airflow 3 architectural change: tasks no longer have direct access to the metadata database. Workers talk to the API server through the Task Execution API / Task SDK. This improves security and isolation and enables running tasks in remote/other environments ("edge" workers) and in other languages over time.

Other notable Airflow 3 items: DAG versioning (UI shows which version of the DAG a run used), assets (renamed from datasets), a new React UI, backfills managed by the scheduler.
problems.lookfor: Correct roles, especially triggerer and DAG processor, and the Airflow 3 isolation change.
problems.followup: What happens if the scheduler goes down mid-run? (Running tasks finish (or are adopted when it restarts); no new tasks scheduled; run multiple schedulers for HA — supported since Airflow 2.)

problems.title: logical_date, data intervals and idempotent tasks
problems.question: A daily DAG runs at 00:30 on 2026-11-22 and loads "yesterday's" data. What is the run's logical_date and data interval? Why should tasks use them instead of datetime.now()?
problems.answer:
With the classic interval-based schedule, a run covers a data interval and starts after it ends. The run that starts on 2026-11-22 covers data_interval_start = 2026-11-21 00:00 to data_interval_end = 2026-11-22 00:00, and its logical_date (formerly execution_date) is the interval start: 2026-11-21. This confuses everyone at first.

Airflow 3 nuance: a raw cron string now defaults to CronTriggerTimetable (create_cron_data_intervals = False) — runs are treated as points in time and logical_date equals the time the run is triggered, with no data interval. If your DAG logic depends on intervals, use CronDataIntervalTimetable explicitly or calculate the window yourself.

Use the run's dates, not the clock:

@task
def load(data_interval_start=None, data_interval_end=None):
    sql = f"""
      DELETE FROM sales WHERE sale_date >= '{data_interval_start:%Y-%m-%d}'
                          AND sale_date <  '{data_interval_end:%Y-%m-%d}';
      INSERT INTO sales SELECT … WHERE … same window …;
    """

(Jinja templates: {{ data_interval_start }}, {{ ds }}.)

Why: idempotency and reruns. If you rerun last Tuesday's run, or backfill March, now() would load today's data again. With interval-based parameters, every run always processes exactly its own window, and reruns overwrite the same window — same input → same output.
problems.lookfor: Interval semantics, the Airflow 3 timetable default change, and idempotency.
problems.followup: A run for 2026-11-21 is cleared and re-run a week later. What data does it process? (Its own interval — if tasks are written properly.)

problems.title: Catchup and backfill
problems.question: You deploy a new DAG with start_date = 2026-01-01 and a daily schedule on 2026-11-22. What happens? How do you backfill historical data safely?
problems.answer:
• catchup=True: the scheduler creates runs for every missed interval since start_date — ~325 runs at once (bounded by max_active_runs).
  • catchup=False: only the latest interval is scheduled.
  • Airflow 3 changed the default: catchup_by_default is now False. In Airflow 2 the default was True, a common source of surprise backfills. Be explicit in every DAG.

Safe backfill:

  • Airflow 3 runs backfills through the scheduler, triggered from the UI, API or CLI (airflow backfill create --dag-id … --from-date … --to-date …), with options such as max active runs and whether to reprocess existing runs.
  • Limit parallelism (max_active_runs, pools) so you don't overload sources or Snowflake.
  • Tasks must be idempotent and parameterised by the run's interval (previous problem).
  • Consider whether a single bulk SQL backfill (one query for the whole year) is far cheaper than 325 daily runs — often it is.
  • Warn downstream consumers; check source system rate limits.

Also: start_date should be a fixed date — never datetime.now() (dynamic start dates confuse the scheduler).
problems.lookfor: Knowing catchup semantics, the Airflow 3 default change, and a responsible backfill plan.
problems.followup: depends_on_past=True — what does it do during a backfill? (A task runs only if its previous run succeeded — enforces order but one failure blocks everything after it.)

problems.title: Choosing an executor
problems.question: Compare LocalExecutor, CeleryExecutor and KubernetesExecutor. Which would you choose for (a) a small team, (b) hundreds of short tasks per minute, (c) tasks with very different dependencies and resource needs?
problems.answer:
executor how tasks run strengths weaknesses
Local subprocesses on the scheduler machine simple, no extra infra limited to one machine
Celery on a pool of long-running workers via a queue (Redis/RabbitMQ) low latency per task, high throughput, worker queues for routing workers must have all dependencies; idle cost; manage the broker
Kubernetes each task in its own pod isolation, per-task resources/images, scales to zero pod start-up latency (seconds), K8s complexity

Choices: (a) Local (or a managed service); (b) Celery — fast start, warm workers; (c) Kubernetes — per-task images and resources.

Airflow 2.10+/3 supports multiple executors at once (configure several and set executor= per task or DAG), replacing the old CeleryKubernetesExecutor hybrid. Managed options (Astronomer, MWAA, Cloud Composer) handle much of this.

Independent of executor: heavy compute should run in the target system (Snowflake, Spark), with Airflow orchestrating — not processing GBs in the worker.
problems.lookfor: Trade-offs tied to workload shape, multi-executor awareness, and "orchestrate, don't process".
problems.followup: Some tasks need GPUs — how do you route them? (Kubernetes pod overrides with node selectors, or a Celery queue with GPU workers.)

problems.title: XCom — what it's for and how people misuse it
problems.question: What is XCom? A teammate passes a 2 GB pandas DataFrame between tasks with XCom. What's wrong, and what should they do?
problems.answer:
XCom ("cross-communication") lets tasks pass small pieces of data: IDs, file paths, row counts, a query id. With the TaskFlow API, return values become XComs automatically:

@task
def extract(ds=None) -> str:          # Airflow injects the run's date
    path = f"s3://bucket/raw/orders/{ds}.parquet"
    # … write the data there …
    return path                    # small: just the location

@task
def load(path: str):
    run_sql(f"COPY INTO raw.orders FROM '{path}' …")

load(extract())

By default XComs are stored in the metadata database. Large values bloat the DB, slow the scheduler/UI, and can hit size limits.

Fix: pass references, not data — write the DataFrame to object storage (or a staging table) and pass the path/table name. If you really need larger XComs, configure an object-storage XCom backend so values are stored in S3/GCS and only a reference goes to the DB.

Even better for data pipelines: don't move data through Airflow workers at all — let Snowflake read the files (COPY) and transform in SQL.
problems.lookfor: "References, not data", the DB impact, and custom XCom backends.
problems.followup: How do you pull an XCom from a task in another DAG? (Possible via xcom_pull(dag_id=…), but it couples DAGs — prefer assets or a shared table/marker.)

problems.title: Sensors: poke, reschedule and deferrable
problems.question: You have 200 sensors waiting for files that may arrive any time within 6 hours. Workers are exhausted and other tasks can't start. Why, and how do you fix it?
problems.answer:
In poke mode, a sensor occupies a worker slot for its whole wait — 200 sensors = 200 slots doing nothing but sleeping.

Options:

  • mode="reschedule" — the sensor checks, then releases its slot and is rescheduled for the next check. Good for long waits with infrequent checks (minutes).
  • Deferrable sensors/operators (deferrable=True on many provider sensors, or *Async variants) — the task hands its wait to the triggerer, an async process that can watch thousands of conditions cheaply. The task resumes on a worker only when the condition is met. Best option for many long waits — requires the triggerer to be running.
  • Event-driven instead of polling: let the file arrival trigger the pipeline (cloud event → Airflow REST API / asset event, or Snowpipe auto-ingest and then an asset-triggered DAG).

Always set timeout (fail after N hours), a sensible poke_interval, and soft_fail if a missing file should skip rather than fail. Use pools to cap the number of concurrent sensors.
problems.lookfor: Explaining slot usage, the triggerer, and preferring event-driven design.
problems.followup: How does a deferrable operator survive a triggerer restart? (Trigger state is stored; triggers are re-created on another triggerer.)

problems.title: Dynamic task mapping
problems.question: Each day, an unknown number of files (0 to 500) arrive. You want one task per file, retried independently. How do you do this without generating DAG code dynamically?
problems.answer:
Dynamic task mapping creates task instances at runtime from a list:

from airflow.sdk import dag, task      # Airflow 3 import path (Airflow 2: from airflow.decorators import dag, task)
import pendulum

@dag(schedule="@daily", start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="UTC"), catchup=False)
def load_files():

    @task
    def list_files(ds=None) -> list[str]:
        return list_s3_keys(prefix=f"raw/orders/{ds}/")   # 0..500 keys

    @task(retries=3, max_active_tis_per_dag=20)           # limit parallel copies
    def load_one(key: str, target: str):
        copy_into_snowflake(key, target)

    load_one.partial(target="RAW.ORDERS").expand(key=list_files())

load_files()
  • .expand() maps over the list; .partial() fixes the constant arguments.
  • Each mapped instance has its own index, logs, retries and state.
  • Zero files → the mapped task is skipped (not failed) — handle downstream with trigger rules if needed.
  • Map over pairs with expand_kwargs, or chain mapped tasks (map → map).
  • Limits: max_map_length config; control concurrency with max_active_tis_per_dag or pools.

Alternative design question: is one task per file right? For 500 small files, a single COPY INTO … PATTERN is far faster and cheaper — use mapping when per-item work is genuinely independent and heavy (API calls per customer, per-tenant pipelines).
problems.lookfor: Correct API, concurrency control, zero-length behaviour, and judging when not to map.
problems.followup: Reduce after mapping — sum row counts from all mapped tasks? (A downstream task receiving the mapped output list: summarize(load_one.expand(...)).)

problems.title: Trigger rules and the branching skip trap
problems.question: A DAG branches: check_day → either full_load or incremental_load → notify. On every run notify is skipped. Why? Fix it, and list the important trigger rules.
problems.answer:
The branch task skips the path not taken. notify has the default trigger rule all_success, which requires all upstream tasks to succeed. One upstream is skipped → notify is skipped too (skips propagate).

Fix:

@task.branch
def check_day(logical_date=None):
    return "full_load" if logical_date.weekday() == 6 else "incremental_load"

@task(trigger_rule="none_failed_min_one_success")
def notify(): ...

check_day() >> [full_load, incremental_load] >> notify()

Trigger rules to know:

rule runs when
all_success (default) all parents succeeded
all_failed all parents failed
all_done all parents finished, any state — cleanup tasks
one_success / one_failed as soon as one parent succeeds / fails
none_failed no parent failed (skips OK)
none_failed_min_one_success no failures and at least one success — the join-after-branch rule
none_skipped no parent skipped
always regardless

Related: ShortCircuitOperator / @task.short_circuit skips everything downstream when a condition is false (e.g. "no new data today").
problems.lookfor: Skip propagation explained, the right rule, and knowing the table.
problems.followup: A cleanup task must run even if the load fails, but the DAG run should still show as failed. How? (trigger_rule="all_done" on cleanup; the run state is determined by leaf tasks — add a final check task, or rely on the failed task being a leaf.)

problems.title: Pools, concurrency and priority
problems.question: Many DAGs call the same vendor API, which allows only 5 concurrent requests. Also, critical finance DAGs must run before ad-hoc ones when resources are tight. How do you configure Airflow?
problems.answer:
• Pools cap concurrency for a shared resource across all DAGs:
# create pool "vendor_api" with 5 slots (UI/CLI: airflow pools set vendor_api 5 "vendor limit")
@task(pool="vendor_api", pool_slots=1, priority_weight=10)
def call_vendor(): ...
  • priority_weight decides which queued tasks get slots first; weight_rule (downstream default, upstream, absolute) controls how weights are summed.
  • DAG-level limits: max_active_runs (concurrent runs of a DAG), max_active_tasks (concurrent tasks in a DAG).
  • Task-level: max_active_tis_per_dag (instances of one task across runs).
  • Global: parallelism (max running tasks for the whole installation per scheduler config), executor capacity, worker concurrency.

For Snowflake-heavy tasks, also consider a pool sized to what your warehouse can handle without queuing (or use multi-cluster warehouses).
problems.lookfor: Pools for shared resources, priority weights, and the levels of concurrency limits.
problems.followup: A task needs 3 "units" of a resource? (pool_slots=3.)

problems.title: DAG parsing performance and top-level code
problems.question: The Airflow UI is slow, DAGs take minutes to appear, and the database is under load. A DAG file starts with rows = snowflake.query("SELECT …") and Variable.get(...) at the top. What's wrong?
problems.answer:
DAG files are parsed repeatedly (by default every ~30 seconds per file) by the DAG processor. Top-level code — anything outside task functions — runs on every parse, not when tasks run. So:

  • Database/API calls at the top level hit Snowflake/the API constantly and slow parsing.
  • Variable.get() at the top level queries the metadata DB on every parse.
  • Heavy imports (pandas, ML libraries) slow parsing too.

Fixes:

  • Move logic into tasks; fetch values at runtime.
  • Use Jinja templates for Variables/connections: "{{ var.value.my_setting }}" — resolved at run time.
  • Import heavy libraries inside the task function.
  • Generate dynamic structures with dynamic task mapping at runtime instead of querying at parse time.
  • Tune min_file_process_interval, use .airflowignore for non-DAG files.
  • Check parse times: airflow dags report / DAG processor stats in the UI.
problems.lookfor: Understanding parse vs run time — the most common Airflow anti-pattern.
problems.followup: You must generate 50 similar DAGs from a config file — acceptable? (Yes, from a static local YAML/JSON file read quickly at parse time; not from a database call.)

problems.title: Data-aware scheduling with assets
problems.question: The marketing DAG runs at 7 am "because ingestion usually finishes by 6:30". Some days ingestion is late and marketing reports use stale data. How do assets solve this?
problems.answer:
Assets (called datasets in Airflow 2) let DAGs be scheduled by data updates instead of time. A producer task declares it updates an asset; consumer DAGs run when the asset is updated.

from airflow.sdk import Asset, dag, task

orders_asset = Asset("snowflake://analytics/raw/orders")

@dag(schedule="@daily", ...)
def ingest():
    @task(outlets=[orders_asset])          # marks the asset as updated on success
    def load_orders(): ...
    load_orders()

@dag(schedule=[orders_asset], ...)         # runs whenever orders_asset is updated
def marketing():
    ...
  • Multiple assets: schedule=(asset_a & asset_b) or (asset_a | asset_b) (conditional expressions).
  • Combine time + data: AssetOrTimeSchedule.
  • External systems can create asset events via the REST API (e.g. "file landed").
  • Assets appear in the UI as lineage between DAGs.
  • Airflow 3.x adds more (asset partitions, watchers that react to external events such as messages in a queue).

The asset URI is just an identifier — Airflow doesn't check the data itself. Pair with data-quality checks before emitting the update.
problems.lookfor: Moving from time-based guessing to data-driven triggering, syntax, and the "identifier only" caveat.
problems.followup: Asset vs ExternalTaskSensor vs TriggerDagRunOperator? (Next problem.)

problems.title: Retries, alerts and failure handling
problems.question: How do you configure a task that calls a flaky API so that transient failures retry automatically, but real failures alert the on-call engineer quickly?
problems.answer:
from datetime import timedelta

default_args = {
    "retries": 3,
    "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=2),
    "retry_exponential_backoff": True,        # 2, 4, 8 … minutes
    "max_retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=30),
    "execution_timeout": timedelta(minutes=20),  # kill hung tasks
    "on_failure_callback": alert_on_call,     # fires after final failure
    "on_retry_callback": log_retry,
}
  • Distinguish transient from permanent errors: for permanent errors (bad credentials, schema mismatch), raise AirflowFailException to fail immediately without retries.
  • execution_timeout prevents hung tasks; DAG-level dagrun_timeout limits whole runs.
  • Alerts: callbacks to Slack/PagerDuty/email (provider notifiers); include DAG, task, logical date, log URL, and a runbook link.
  • Retries require idempotent tasks — a retry must not double-load data.
  • Missed deadlines: SLA misses were removed in Airflow 3; newer versions add deadline alerts to notify when a run hasn't finished by a time.
problems.lookfor: Backoff, timeouts, failing fast on permanent errors, and idempotency.
problems.followup: Retry an API call within one task several times before failing the task? (Use a retry library (tenacity) inside the task for fast transient retries; Airflow retries for longer outages.)

problems.title: Cross-DAG dependencies
problems.question: DAG B must run after DAG A finishes. Compare ExternalTaskSensor, TriggerDagRunOperator and assets. Which do you prefer?
problems.answer:
approach how pros cons
ExternalTaskSensor (in B) B waits for a task/DAG in A with the same logical date (or an offset) B keeps its own schedule schedules must align; misaligned dates → waits forever; occupies slots unless deferrable
TriggerDagRunOperator (in A) A triggers B at the end explicit, immediate A must know about B (tight coupling); B has no schedule of its own
Assets A updates an asset; B is scheduled on it loose coupling; many consumers; lineage in UI event-based only; logical dates differ between DAGs

Preference: assets for most data dependencies (producer doesn't need to know consumers). TriggerDagRun for a controller/"pipeline of pipelines" pattern where A deliberately orchestrates B with parameters (conf). ExternalTaskSensor mostly in legacy setups or when date alignment matters strongly.
problems.lookfor: Coupling and date-alignment trade-offs.
problems.followup: B depends on A and C, which run at different times? (Assets with schedule=(asset_a & asset_c).)

problems.title: Connections, variables and secrets
problems.question: How should DAGs store credentials for Snowflake and APIs? Where do Variables fit? How do you keep secrets out of logs and git?
problems.answer:
• Connections hold credentials and endpoints, referenced by conn_id in hooks/operators: SnowflakeHook(snowflake_conn_id="snowflake_prod"). Never hard-code credentials in DAG files.
  • Secrets backend (production standard): store connections/variables in AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault; Airflow reads them at runtime. Rotation happens in one place.
  • Environment variables AIRFLOW_CONN_<ID> / AIRFLOW_VAR_<NAME> for local dev and containers.
  • Variables for small non-secret config (feature flags, thresholds). Read them in templates or inside tasks — not at the top level.
  • Airflow masks values of connection passwords and variables whose names contain words like password, secret, api_key in logs and the UI; don't print secrets yourself.
  • Snowflake: use key-pair authentication (or OAuth) for service users, with least-privilege roles.
problems.lookfor: Secrets backend, no hard-coding, masking, and service-account auth.
problems.followup: Different credentials per environment with the same DAG code? (Same conn_id, different secrets per environment's backend path.)

problems.title: Testing Airflow DAGs
problems.question: How do you test Airflow DAGs before they reach production?
problems.answer:
1. DAG integrity test (run in CI) — every DAG imports without errors, has no cycles, follows rules:
from airflow.models import DagBag

def test_dags_load():
    bag = DagBag(dag_folder="dags/", include_examples=False)
    assert not bag.import_errors, bag.import_errors

def test_rules():
    bag = DagBag(dag_folder="dags/", include_examples=False)
    for dag_id, dag in bag.dags.items():
        assert dag.tags, f"{dag_id} needs tags"
        assert dag.default_args.get("retries", 0) >= 1, f"{dag_id} needs retries"
  1. Unit tests for business logic — keep logic in plain Python functions/modules, tested with pytest, mocking hooks/APIs. Thin DAG files = easy testing.
  2. dag.test() — runs a whole DAG in one process locally for debugging (no scheduler needed).
  3. Lint: ruff with Airflow rules (AIR rules flag deprecated/removed Airflow 3 APIs).
  4. Integration tests in a staging environment against dev Snowflake schemas.
  5. Containerised local env (e.g. Astro CLI or docker-compose) identical to production images.
problems.lookfor: Layered testing, thin DAGs with logic in modules, CI automation.
problems.followup: How do you test a task that uses data_interval_start? (Call the function directly with a fixed datetime, or dag.test(logical_date=…).)

problems.title: Upgrading from Airflow 2 to Airflow 3
problems.question: You own 400 DAGs on Airflow 2.x. Plan the upgrade to Airflow 3. What breaks, and how do you de-risk it?
problems.answer:
Main breaking changes to check:

  • No direct metadata DB access from tasks. Code using settings.Session, querying DagRun/TaskInstance models directly, or custom operators that touch the DB must move to the REST API / Task SDK.
  • SubDAGs removed → TaskGroups or assets.
  • Scheduling defaults: catchup defaults to False; schedule_interval and timetable args removed (use schedule); raw cron strings now use CronTriggerTimetable (no data intervals by default) — DAGs relying on data_interval_* behaviour need review.
  • execution_date and some context keys removed — use logical_date / data interval values.
  • Imports moved: many airflow.operators.* / airflow.sensors.* moved to the standard provider; authoring via airflow.sdk.
  • Auth/UI: new React UI; Simple Auth manager by default — FAB-based auth needs the FAB provider.
  • The DAG processor runs as a separate component; webserver replaced by API server.
  • SLA misses removed.

Plan:

  1. Upgrade to the latest 2.x first; fix all deprecation warnings.
  2. Run ruff Airflow rules (AIR30x mandatory, AIR31x recommended) across the repo; fix automatically where possible. Run the config upgrade checker.
  3. Inventory risky DAGs: DB access, SubDAGs, custom plugins/operators, interval-dependent logic.
  4. Stand up Airflow 3 in parallel (new environment); migrate DAGs in waves by domain; compare outputs.
  5. DAG integrity tests and dag.test() in CI against Airflow 3 images.
